lessons.title: Conversations that build trust
lessons.description: Listen with intention. Explain with clarity. Make every interaction matter.
steps: Start with the person
Introduce yourself and your role. Ask what matters most today, then listen without interrupting. Acknowledge the emotion before moving to the clinical agenda.
Make understanding a shared responsibility
Use plain language and small chunks of information. Ask: “To check that I explained this clearly, how will you describe the plan in your own words?” Re-explain and check again when needed.
Close the loop
Agree on the next step, who owns it, and when it will happen. Explain follow-up and locally appropriate safety-net advice. Use a qualified interpreter when needed rather than assuming understanding.
lessons.takeaway: Teach-back is a check on how clearly you explained—not a test of the patient.
lessons.question: Priya, a ward nurse, has just explained a new discharge plan to Mr Okafor. His taxi is due in ten minutes and he has nodded throughout without asking anything. What most directly checks how clearly she explained the next step?
answers: Ask, “So I know I’ve explained it well, how will you describe the plan to your daughter tonight?”
Summarise the three main points again, slowly, and ask whether he has any questions before the taxi arrives.
Give him the printed discharge summary, point out the key section and ask him to ring the ward if anything is unclear.
lessons.feedback: Asking him to put the plan in his own words puts the check on your explanation, not on him. Any gap shows while he is still on the ward and you can fix it.
lessons.reflect: What is one phrase you could replace with clearer, more human language in your next conversation?
rationales: Asking him to put the plan in his own words puts the check on your explanation, not on him. Any gap shows while he is still on the ward and you can fix it.
A slower repeat feels thorough, but “any questions?” invites a polite no. Nodding is not evidence of understanding, so try a teach-back prompt instead.
Written information helps later, but it cannot show what he has understood now. Use the leaflet to support a teach-back check rather than to replace one.
lessons.visualAlt: Practitioner listening as an older adult explains their understanding.

lessons.title: Small checks. Safer care.
lessons.description: Build safer habits around medications, transitions, and everyday clinical decisions.
steps: Pause before acting
Use the identifiers required by your organization. Check allergy information and the intended task against the appropriate record; location or familiarity is not a substitute for identification.
Reconcile at transitions
Compare the best available medication history with the current plan. Clarify unexplained differences with the responsible prescriber or pharmacist; do not guess. Involve the patient or caregiver.
Make uncertainty visible
If an order, dose, route, or product is unclear, pause and clarify through your local process before proceeding. Report near misses through the organizational system so the team can learn.
lessons.takeaway: A pause to resolve uncertainty is a safety action, not a delay to apologize for.
lessons.question: A man arrives on the ward from a care home. The transfer sheet lists a blood-thinning tablet that his daughter says was stopped last week, and the GP summary does not mention it. The drug round starts in ten minutes. What best addresses the uncertainty?
answers: Go with the transfer sheet, since it is the most formal document, and note the daughter’s comment in his file.
Ask him which tablets he took this morning and follow his account, as it is the most recent information.
Hold that item and ask the pharmacist or prescriber to reconcile the three sources before it is given.
lessons.feedback: Reconciliation resolves a conflict between records and the patient’s account; it does not pick a winner by guesswork. Pausing the one uncertain item protects him while the answer is found.
lessons.reflect: Where in your workflow would a deliberate pause prevent a common near miss?
rationales: A formal document can still be out of date. Recording the daughter’s comment without acting on it leaves the discrepancy unresolved.
His account matters, but memory and confusion on transfer can both mislead. It is one source to compare, not the tie-breaker.
Reconciliation resolves a conflict between records and the patient’s account; it does not pick a winner by guesswork. Pausing the one uncertain item protects him while the answer is found.

lessons.title: Empathy in everyday practice
lessons.description: Bring curiosity, respect, and compassion to the moments that need them most.
steps: Notice without assuming
Observe words, tone, and hesitation. Ask “What concerns you most?” rather than inferring feelings from appearance, age, culture, or diagnosis.
Acknowledge the experience
Try “That sounds like a lot to manage.” Allow silence. Validation does not require agreeing with every request or making promises outside your role.
Invite partnership
Explore the person’s priorities, practical barriers, and preferred involvement in decisions. Share options honestly, including uncertainty, and agree on an achievable next step.
lessons.takeaway: Empathy is curiosity put into words and followed by action.
lessons.question: Mrs Hughes, 78, was given a new daily exercise plan after her fall. At review she sighs and says, “It’s all a bit much, really.” You have ten minutes. What is the most useful response before you offer any solution?
answers: “Let’s cut it down to the easiest exercises so it feels more manageable for you.”
“It sounds like a lot to manage. Which part is hardest at the moment?”
“I know it’s hard, but sticking with it is what will get you back on your feet.”
lessons.feedback: Naming the feeling and asking which part is hard shows you are curious rather than assuming. Her answer then tells you where to adapt the plan.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you made an assumption. What curious question could you ask instead? Do not include identifying details.
rationales: Trimming the plan may be right in the end, but offering it first guesses at the problem. It might be the pain, the time or the stairs.
Naming the feeling and asking which part is hard shows you are curious rather than assuming. Her answer then tells you where to adapt the plan.
Explaining why the plan matters can sound like a reprimand. Understand what is getting in her way before making the case for the plan.

lessons.title: A handover that gets heard
lessons.description: Use SBAR and closed-loop communication to make the next step unmistakable.
steps: Lead with situation and urgency
Identify yourself, your role, the patient using approved identifiers, and the immediate concern. State urgency clearly. Escalate emergencies immediately through local procedures.
Give relevant background and assessment
Keep background concise. Share recent changes, relevant context, and your assessment within your scope. Separate observed facts from interpretation.
Make a clear recommendation
Ask explicitly for the review or action you need and by when. Confirm the recipient’s understanding, ownership, and escalation plan if help does not arrive.
lessons.takeaway: A good handover transfers responsibility, not just information.
lessons.question: At 02:00 you give an SBAR about a patient whose breathing has worsened. The on-call doctor says, “OK, noted, thanks,” and starts to hang up without saying whether she is coming. What best establishes a shared plan?
answers: “Thanks. I will record in the notes that you have been informed about his breathing, with the time of this call.”
“Just to be sure it was clear: his breathing is faster than an hour ago and he is looking more tired.”
“Before you go, who will see him and by when, and who should I call if he worsens before then?”
lessons.feedback: Ownership, timing and a contingency turn an acknowledged message into a shared plan. Asking before she hangs up is the last chance to close the loop.
lessons.reflect: Which part of your usual handover is least explicit: urgency, assessment, ownership, or next step?
rationales: Documenting the call is useful but does not tell you who will act. A record that someone was informed is not a plan.
Repeating the findings checks that the message was heard, not that anyone will respond. The recommendation and ownership are what is still missing.
Ownership, timing and a contingency turn an acknowledged message into a shared plan. Asking before she hangs up is the last chance to close the loop.

lessons.title: Infection prevention, every time
lessons.description: Turn standard precautions into consistent, situation-aware habits.
steps: Apply standard precautions to everyone
Do not wait for an infection diagnosis. Match hand hygiene, PPE, injection safety, and equipment handling to the task and anticipated exposure.
Choose protection for the exposure
Assess potential contact with blood, body fluids, mucosa, and nonintact skin. Add transmission-based precautions when indicated by local policy and current organism-specific guidance.
Protect the next interaction
Perform hand hygiene at required moments; gloves do not replace it. Remove PPE safely and clean or appropriately reprocess shared equipment before the next patient.
lessons.takeaway: Standard precautions are the starting point for every patient—not a label reserved for known infections.
lessons.question: Between two patients on a bay, the shared blood-pressure cuff looks spotless. The first patient had no known infection and the next is waiting. What determines whether it is ready to reuse?
answers: The cleaning or reprocessing step your local policy sets for that equipment between patients.
Whether the first patient was on additional precautions, since only then does the cuff need cleaning.
Whether anything visible is on it, because a clean-looking cuff has not touched anything harmful.
lessons.feedback: Standard precautions apply to everyone, so reuse follows the approved process for that item, not how it looks or who used it.
lessons.reflect: Which frequently touched piece of shared equipment needs a clearer cleaning handoff in your workplace?
rationales: Standard precautions apply to everyone, so reuse follows the approved process for that item, not how it looks or who used it.
Waiting for an infection label misses the point of standard precautions. Equipment is prepared for reuse in the same way for every patient.
Contamination is often invisible. A visual check cannot replace the approved cleaning process.

lessons.title: Think clearly under uncertainty
lessons.description: Recognize assumptions, seek disconfirming evidence, and ask for a second view.
steps: Separate observations from interpretation
State what you know, how reliable it is, and what is missing. Do not let an early label replace ongoing assessment.
Take a diagnostic pause
Ask: “What else could explain this? What does not fit? What important alternative should I not miss?” Use current, locally approved pathways and decision support within your scope.
Reassess and safety-net

Discuss uncertainty and the follow-up plan with the responsible team and patient. Specify what change warrants review and who will act on pending results. Seek senior help when concern exceeds your role or confidence.
lessons.takeaway: Confidence is useful; a clear plan for uncertainty is safer.
lessons.question: A man in the emergency department was labelled “anxiety, chest tightness” at triage. An hour later his observations have changed and he says the pain now spreads to his arm. What best supports a safe reassessment?
answers: Take another full set of observations, and speak to the doctor only if they continue to worsen.
Tell the doctor what no longer fits the anxiety explanation and ask the team to consider what else it could be.
Ask the triage nurse whether she still thinks anxiety is the most likely explanation before going any further.
lessons.feedback: Naming the mismatch out loud and opening up alternatives counters anchoring on the first label. It keeps the decision with the responsible team.
lessons.reflect: What question can you add to your next case discussion to challenge an early assumption?
rationales: More observations are not wrong, but waiting to see a worse trend delays a concern you already have. Share the new information now.
Naming the mismatch out loud and opening up alternatives counters anchoring on the first label. It keeps the decision with the responsible team.
Asking the person who made the first judgement tends to bring back the same answer. Take the mismatch to the responsible clinician instead.

lessons.title: Speak up for safer teams
lessons.description: Raise concerns with clarity—and make it easier for others to do the same.
steps: Name the concern respectfully
Use observable facts and patient-focused language. TeamSTEPPS CUS can structure a concern: “I am concerned. I am uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.”
Persist through the appropriate route
If your concern is not acknowledged, repeat it clearly and escalate according to your local policy. In an emergency, activate the appropriate response without delaying for a perfect script.
Invite and thank the next voice
Leaders and colleagues can ask, “What are we missing?” Thank people who raise concerns. Debrief systems and decisions without humiliation or blame.
lessons.takeaway: Speaking up is a team skill. Receiving a concern well is the other half.
lessons.question: During a busy handover on a surgical ward, a newly qualified nurse interrupts to say, “I’m worried Mr Lee’s wound dressing is wetter than the chart suggests.” The consultant round starts in five minutes. What best supports speaking up?
answers: Thank her, ask what she has seen, and have someone check the patient now before the handover carries on.
Ask her to jot the concern down so it can be discussed properly once the handover is over.
Explain the reasoning behind the current plan, then ask whether that changes her view.
lessons.feedback: Receiving a concern well is half of speaking up. Thanking her and checking straight away shows concerns are welcome and keeps the patient first.
lessons.reflect: How will you respond the next time someone questions your plan?
rationales: Receiving a concern well is half of speaking up. Thanking her and checking straight away shows concerns are welcome and keeps the patient first.
Deferring may feel orderly, but it tells her that a safety concern can wait for a convenient moment. Quick checks cost minutes; missed ones cost far more.
Justifying the plan first can sound like “you are wrong”. Listen to what she observed before you defend anything.

lessons.title: Decisions made together
lessons.description: Connect evidence and options with what matters to the individual.
steps: Make the choice visible
Invite participation and explain that there are options when a genuine choice exists. Ask how the patient wants to be involved and what matters to them.
Compare benefits, harms, and uncertainty
Use balanced, plain language and reliable decision aids. When communicating probabilities, use consistent denominators and time frames; avoid presenting relative benefit alone.
Agree, document, and revisit
Check understanding, explore preferences, and agree on a plan with the responsible clinician. Document the discussion and arrange a way to review the decision if circumstances change.
lessons.takeaway: The best available evidence and the person’s priorities belong in the same conversation.
lessons.question: Mr Banks, 71, has two reasonable options for his painful knee: twelve weeks of physiotherapy or a referral for surgical opinion. He lives alone and is his wife’s main carer. What should shape the next conversation?
answers: Which option most patients of his age and circumstances have chosen, as that is the best guide to what works.
Which option is simpler for the team to arrange and explain, so the plan runs smoothly.
How each option’s benefits, risks and uncertainty fit with his caring role and what matters to him.
lessons.feedback: Shared decisions bring the evidence and the person’s priorities into one conversation. His caring role may change which trade-off matters most.
lessons.reflect: What could you ask to uncover a priority that is not visible in the clinical record?
rationales: What others chose says little about what he values. Popularity is not the same as fit.
Convenience for the service can quietly steer the choice. The options should be compared on his terms, with the real trade-offs.
Shared decisions bring the evidence and the person’s priorities into one conversation. His caring role may change which trade-off matters most.

lessons.title: AI literacy, clinical responsibility
lessons.description: Use emerging tools thoughtfully. Verify outputs. Protect trust and privacy.
steps: Know the tool and its limits
Check intended use, organizational approval, and whether it has been evaluated for your setting. A fluent answer can still be wrong, incomplete, or biased.
Protect sensitive information
Do not enter patient-identifiable or confidential information into unapproved tools. Follow organizational privacy, consent, security, and data-governance requirements.
Verify before relying
Independently check clinical claims and references using authoritative, current sources. Keep qualified human oversight and follow your organization’s disclosure and documentation policies.
lessons.takeaway: A convincing output is not verified evidence. Accountability does not transfer to the tool.
lessons.question: A colleague pastes an AI-generated summary into the team chat before your medicines safety meeting. It says a recent trial shows a benefit and cites “Hartley et al., 2023”, which nobody recognises. What is the strongest verification step?
answers: Ask the tool for the full reference and the relevant quote, and accept it if it can supply both.
Find the original paper through a library or database and check it says what the summary claims.
Check that the journal looks credible and the year fits, then share it with a note that it needs review.
lessons.feedback: Only the source itself can show whether the claim is supported. AI tools can produce convincing citations that do not exist or say something else.
lessons.reflect: What is one clear boundary you need before using a digital or AI tool in your work?
rationales: The same tool can generate a convincing reference and quote. Asking it to vouch for itself is not independent checking.
Only the source itself can show whether the claim is supported. AI tools can produce convincing citations that do not exist or say something else.
A plausible journal and date are easy to fake and say nothing about the claim. Circulating it first lets an unchecked claim spread.

lessons.title: Care for the person providing care
lessons.description: Notice strain, protect recovery, and build a practical support plan.
steps: Notice the load without judgment
Recognize changes in concentration, sleep, mood, or connection. Fatigue is not a character flaw; it can be a signal that workload and recovery need attention.
Make one feasible adjustment
Where possible, take a brief pause, meet a basic need, or ask a colleague for support. Individual habits do not replace safe staffing, rest, and organizational responsibility.
Use support early

Discuss workload and safety concerns with appropriate supervisors or occupational health. If distress persists or affects functioning, seek qualified help. For immediate danger, use local emergency support.
lessons.takeaway: Sustainable care needs both personal support and working conditions that make safe practice possible.
lessons.question: Aisha, a healthcare assistant, tells you she has not slept properly for weeks and keeps losing track mid-task. The shift has started and the ward is short-staffed. What addresses both the immediate and the continuing concern?
answers: Suggest a quiet break and say you will check in with how she feels at the end of the shift.
Share the trust wellbeing leaflet and ask her to pick one idea from it to try this week.
Offer help now, like a short break, and encourage her to raise the workload with her manager.
lessons.feedback: Fatigue is a signal, not a flaw. Immediate support helps today, and the manager conversation addresses the conditions behind it.
lessons.reflect: Who can you approach for practical support, and what specific request could you make?
rationales: A break helps for now, but with nothing to follow up the longer-term picture is left alone. Pair the break with the conversation about workload.
Resources can help, but handing them over leaves the load on her. Individual habits do not replace safe staffing and rest.
Fatigue is a signal, not a flaw. Immediate support helps today, and the manager conversation addresses the conditions behind it.

lessons.title: Curiosity over assumptions
lessons.description: Recognize barriers and make room for every patient’s voice.
steps: Ask, do not presume
Ask about preferred name, language, communication needs, and what would make care more accessible. Avoid assumptions based on identity or background.
Make understanding accessible
Offer qualified interpretation and accessible formats through your service. Speak directly to the patient. Ask about hearing, vision, literacy, and practical needs sensitively.
Check the real-world plan
Explore cost, transport, support, and other barriers. Invite the patient’s preferences and work with the relevant team to adapt the plan while preserving safe care.
lessons.takeaway: Equity starts with noticing who a standard approach might leave out.
lessons.question: Mr Nowak agrees to a new monitoring plan through his adult son, who speaks for him at the surgery. Nobody has asked about language, reading or how he gets to appointments. What is the best next step?
answers: Ask Mr Nowak how he likes to receive information and whether an interpreter would help.
Give him the standard leaflet and ask his son to go through it with him when they get home.
Check he is happy to continue in English, then book the follow-up appointment if he says yes.
lessons.feedback: Asking him directly puts him at the centre and uncovers communication and access needs that his agreement may be hiding.
lessons.reflect: What is one barrier your standard appointment process may create, and who can help change it?
rationales: Asking him directly puts him at the centre and uncovers communication and access needs that his agreement may be hiding.
This assumes the leaflet and his son will suffice. A family member can help, but is not a substitute for qualified support or for asking him.
Asking is a good start, but a polite yes may reflect reluctance to be a bother. Explore what support would help, including practical access.

lessons.title: Turn reflection into better systems
lessons.description: Learn from near misses and test small, measurable changes.
steps: Describe the process, not a person to blame
Identify where the workflow becomes fragile. Involve the people who do the work and the patients affected. Use the approved incident process for safety events.
Choose a small, safe test
Define a specific aim, a measure, and a limited change to try with the appropriate approval. Check for unintended effects as well as intended benefits.
Review and adapt
Compare what happened with what you expected. Decide with the team whether to adapt, repeat, or stop the test. Share learning without identifiable patient details.
lessons.takeaway: A useful reflection ends with a small action, an owner, and a way to learn whether it helped.
lessons.question: Task owners are often not named at handover on your ward. The manager suggests adding a mandatory “owner” column to the handover sheet across the whole hospital next month. Which next step supports learning from a small test?
answers: Roll the new column out across the service and ask staff for feedback after a month.
Try a limited change on one shift for two weeks, with a measure and a check for added time.
Repeat the handover refresher session and count how many staff attend.
lessons.feedback: A small, time-limited test with a measure and a balancing check lets you learn what works before committing the whole service.
lessons.reflect: What small workflow improvement could your team test, and how would you know whether it helped?
rationales: A wide launch gives you opinions, but little evidence of whether it helped or caused problems. Test on a small scale first.
A small, time-limited test with a measure and a balancing check lets you learn what works before committing the whole service.
Counting attendance measures activity, not whether owners are being named. Choose a measure that shows the effect you want.

lessons.title: Health literacy is a shared responsibility
lessons.description: Reduce jargon, information overload and the hidden effort of navigating care.
steps: Design for everyone
Understanding can change with stress, unfamiliar language and a new setting. Use clear information for everyone rather than trying to identify who appears to have low literacy.
Make the next action visible
Prioritise what the person needs to do next. Use everyday words, a short written summary and accessible formats. Ask about language and communication preferences.
Check your explanation
Use an open teach-back invitation, listen for gaps, rephrase and check again. Ask whether the plan can work with the person’s practical circumstances.
lessons.outcome: Recognise an information barrier and redesign one explanation.
lessons.takeaway: An explanation succeeds when the person can use it.
lessons.reflect: Which instruction in your service needs a clearer next action?
example: A fictional appointment message lists several unfamiliar abbreviations.
The instructions are standard; please read them again.
Let us put this into everyday words and identify your next step together.
Ask a person to explain the next step after one short explanation.
checks: A person follows a conversation until new abbreviations appear. What helps?
Replace abbreviations, explain one action and check understanding.
Repeat the abbreviations more slowly.
Assume agreement means understanding.
What should guide an accessible format?
The person’s communication needs and preferences.
The cheapest format in every case.
How confident the person appears.
A clear explanation still produces an impractical plan. What next?
Explore practical barriers and involve the appropriate team.
Give the same explanation again.
Label the person unmotivated.
lessons.question: During a discharge talk at 16:30, a woman who has followed everything so far goes quiet when you say “PRN”, “U&Es” and “OPD follow-up”. She has her coat on and her lift is waiting outside. What helps most?
answers: Swap the abbreviations for everyday words, focus on one next action, and ask her to say it back.
Slow down and say the abbreviations more clearly, so she can pick up the terms as you go along.
Carry on at the same pace, since she was following well and has not asked you to stop or explain.
rationales: Plain words, one clear action and a teach-back check make the explanation usable. Her sudden quiet may be the only sign she has lost the thread.
Slower jargon is still jargon. Replacing the terms with everyday words helps far more than repeating them.
Silence after unfamiliar terms is often confusion in disguise. Agreement or quiet is not evidence of understanding, and many people will not interrupt.
lessons.feedback: Plain words, one clear action and a teach-back check make the explanation usable. Her sudden quiet may be the only sign she has lost the thread.

lessons.title: Make numbers mean something
lessons.description: Read absolute risk, relative change and uncertainty without being misled.
steps: Start with the denominator
Ask how many people, over what time, and with which outcome. Compare the same population, denominator and period. A count without a denominator is hard to interpret.
Show both sides of a change
In a fictional example, an outcome falls from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100. That is 2 percentage points less, and a 50% relative reduction. These describe the same change in different ways.
Check transferability
Examine the study setting, design and uncertainty. An association is not automatically a causal effect, and a result from one setting is not a forecast for another.
lessons.outcome: Explain a risk change using an absolute difference and a consistent denominator.
lessons.takeaway: Always ask: compared with what, among whom, and over how long?
lessons.reflect: Where could a percentage in your work benefit from a denominator?
example: A fictional flyer says an intervention halves an outcome.
A 50% reduction means 50 fewer people in every 100.
What were the starting and ending risks, time period and population?
Check the absolute figures behind one relative-risk claim.
checks: A fictional risk changes from 4% to 2%. What is the absolute reduction?
2 percentage points.
50 percentage points.
2% of the original 4%.
Two rates use different follow-up periods. What is needed?
A comparable time frame before interpreting the difference.
The larger percentage alone.
A more impressive chart.
A before-and-after study shows improvement. What is justified?
An observed association, with design limitations considered.
Proof that the change caused every improvement.
A guarantee of the same effect locally.
lessons.question: A leaflet for a new screening test says it “halves the chance of a serious complication”. The study behind it shows the risk falling from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100 over five years. A patient asks what the actual reduction is. What do you tell her?
answers: 50 percentage points, because the risk has gone from 4 down to 2, which is half of what it was.
2% of the original 4%, which is a very small proportion of the risk and only a minor change.
2 percentage points, which means 2 fewer people in every 100 over the five years.
rationales: Fifty per cent is the relative reduction, not the absolute one. Mixing them up makes the benefit look far larger than it is.
Two per cent of four is about 0.08 per cent, which is not what happened. The risk fell from 4% to 2%, a drop of 2 percentage points.
The absolute reduction is the difference between the two risks: 4 minus 2. “Halves” describes the same change in relative terms.
lessons.feedback: The absolute reduction is the difference between the two risks: 4 minus 2. “Halves” describes the same change in relative terms.

lessons.title: Design around human limits
lessons.description: Recognise interruptions, memory load and fragile systems before blaming people.
steps: Look at work as it happens
Map the actual task, tools, environment, handoffs and competing demands. Ask the people doing the work where the process becomes difficult.
Build a reliable support
Reduce unnecessary complexity. Use a visible task owner, a clear cue or an approved checklist at the point of work. A reminder to concentrate is a weak response to a recurring design problem.
Test for new burden
Try a limited approved change and check its effect on errors, time and workarounds. Include people who might experience new barriers.
lessons.outcome: Identify a system condition and propose a small testable safeguard.
lessons.takeaway: A reliable process supports people when attention and memory are stretched.
lessons.reflect: Which recurring interruption deserves a system change?
example: A fictional team misses a task after repeated interruptions.
Everyone needs to remember better.
Let us map the interruption and test a visible task cue with a named owner.
Map one fragile step with the people who perform it.
checks: A recurring omission survives repeated reminders. What is useful?
Study the workflow and test a support at the fragile step.
Send a stronger reminder.
Identify the least experienced person.
What is a balancing measure for a new checklist?
Added time or duplication caused by the checklist.
Only the number of printed copies.
Only attendance at the launch.
Why involve people doing the work?
They can reveal constraints absent from the written procedure.
They can guarantee the solution will work.
They replace the need for approval.
lessons.question: On a medical ward, the end-of-shift check that bed alarms are switched on keeps being missed. Three reminder emails and a team talk have not changed it, and the night shift is starting to feel blamed. What is a useful next step?
answers: Send a firmer reminder and ask each nurse to confirm in writing that they have read it.
Watch the task as it happens, ask staff where it gets difficult, and test a cue at that step.
Look at who was on shift when it was missed and arrange extra training for those nurses.
rationales: A stronger reminder is still a reminder. A repeated omission points to a design problem, not a concentration problem.
When reminders fail, look at the work itself. Watching it and asking those who do it reveals a fragile step a support can fix.
Singling out individuals assumes the cause is personal. If several people miss the same step, the process is the likelier culprit.
lessons.feedback: When reminders fail, look at the work itself. Watching it and asking those who do it reveals a fragile step a support can fix.

lessons.title: Medication lists across transitions
lessons.description: Recognise discrepancies and clarify the intended plan with the responsible team.
steps: Compare credible accounts
Use the approved reconciliation process to compare available records and the person’s account. Identify an unexplained omission, duplication or change.
Clarify, do not prescribe by inference
Record the uncertainty and route it to the responsible clinician or pharmacist. Do not decide to start, stop or change a medicine from this learning exercise.
Communicate the verified plan
Ensure the agreed resolution reaches the authorised record, receiving team and person through the approved workflow. Confirm ownership of unresolved items.
lessons.outcome: Distinguish a discrepancy from a verified medication decision.
lessons.takeaway: A discrepancy is a question to resolve, not an instruction to guess.
lessons.reflect: Who owns unresolved medication questions at your handover?
example: Two fictional lists disagree about whether Medicine A is current.
The newest list must be right.
The accounts conflict. I will seek verification through the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
Clarify ownership of a reconciliation question.
checks: A medicine appears on only one transfer list. What can you conclude?
There is a discrepancy requiring appropriate verification.
The medicine should be stopped.
The older record is wrong.
Which person’s account is relevant?
The patient or caregiver, alongside approved reliable sources.
Only the newest computer entry.
Only the receiving team’s assumptions.
Verification resolves a discrepancy. What follows?
Communicate and document the agreed plan through the approved process.
Keep the answer in memory.
Delete the uncertainty without communicating.
lessons.question: A resident comes back to the care home after a hospital stay. A medicine for his blood pressure is on the discharge list but is not on the care home’s own record, and the senior carer asks you what that means. What can you conclude?
answers: The hospital probably stopped it, so the care home record is right and the discharge list can be set aside.
The care home missed it, so it should be added now, since the hospital list is the more recent document.
There is a discrepancy that needs verifying with the pharmacist or prescriber before anything changes.
rationales: This guesses at the reason. A medicine missing from one record may have been left off by mistake.
Newer does not always mean correct, and adding a medicine by inference is a prescribing decision. Ask the responsible clinician.
A mismatch is a question to resolve, not an instruction. Verification comes before any start, stop or change to a medicine.
lessons.feedback: A mismatch is a question to resolve, not an instruction. Verification comes before any start, stop or change to a medicine.

lessons.title: Recognise a change. Escalate clearly.
lessons.description: Make changes, urgency and responsibility explicit without waiting for certainty.
steps: Notice the change
Describe the observed change and relevant context within your role. Do not let a reassuring label replace current observations or the person’s expressed concern.
Use the immediate local route
For urgent concern, use the local emergency or escalation pathway immediately. A communication mnemonic must not become a waiting sequence or substitute for clinical assessment.
Keep the loop open until action is clear
Confirm the receiving person, expected response and contingency if help does not arrive. Re-escalate through local policy if the concern remains unresolved.
lessons.outcome: Give a clear change-and-concern message with ownership and contingency.
lessons.takeaway: Communicate significant concern before certainty arrives.
lessons.reflect: How do you confirm that a concern has an action owner?
example: A fictional record says stable but new information is concerning.
The earlier note was reassuring, so I will wait.
There is a new change and I am concerned. I will activate the appropriate local response now.
Review where to find your local escalation pathway.
checks: Urgent concern emerges during a practice handover. What takes priority?
The immediate local escalation pathway within your role.
Finishing a perfect SBAR script.
Waiting for the next routine handover.
What does a reassuring earlier note establish?
Earlier context; it does not negate a new change.
That reassessment is unnecessary.
That any new concern is incorrect.
Acknowledgment arrives but no action owner is named. What remains?
Confirm responsibility, response timing and contingency.
Assume the task is assigned.
End the conversation to avoid repetition.
lessons.question: During a routine 20:00 handover on an older-people ward, you notice Mrs Pike’s breathing is faster and she seems newly confused. The coordinator is halfway through the SBAR for bed 12 and the oncoming team is waiting. What takes priority?
answers: Interrupt and use the immediate local escalation pathway for Mrs Pike, then return to the handover.
Let the coordinator finish a clear SBAR for bed 12, so the handover is complete before you speak up.
Write the change on the handover sheet and make sure it is raised at the next routine review.
rationales: An urgent concern does not wait for a tidy script. Escalating first keeps the patient’s safety ahead of the handover process.
A complete handover matters, but a few minutes of delay can matter more to Mrs Pike. Communicate significant concern before certainty arrives.
A note is not a call for help. Writing it down and waiting leaves a change in condition without anyone acting on it.
lessons.feedback: An urgent concern does not wait for a tidy script. Escalating first keeps the patient’s safety ahead of the handover process.

lessons.title: Protect information. Preserve trust.
lessons.description: Choose approved channels, minimise disclosure and check digital outputs.
steps: Know the purpose and channel
Use organisationally approved systems and authorised access for a defined purpose. Consult current information-governance policy rather than inferring permission from convenience.
Minimise what is shared
Names are not the only identifiers. Dates, locations, rare details and combinations can identify someone. Removing a name alone does not establish anonymity.
Verify and report
Independently check material before relying on it. If information is sent to the wrong place, follow the local incident process promptly and preserve relevant facts.
lessons.outcome: Recognise an unsafe information-sharing assumption and choose an approved route.
lessons.takeaway: Useful information still needs an authorised purpose and destination.
lessons.reflect: What digital convenience needs a clearer boundary in your work?
example: A fictional note without a name is proposed for a public tool.
No name means no privacy concern.
Other details may identify the person; we need an approved workflow before sharing.
Identify the approved information-governance contact for your setting.
checks: A note has no name but includes a rare event and location. Is it anonymous?
Not necessarily; combinations of details can identify someone.
Yes, because the name was removed.
Yes, if shared only once.
A file is sent to the wrong recipient. What helps?
Follow the local reporting and containment process promptly.
Wait to see whether anyone complains.
Assume deletion resolves every consequence.
A digital output is fluent and well formatted. What does that establish?
Presentation quality; accuracy and suitability still require checks.
Independent verification.
Organisational permission to use it.
lessons.question: A student nurse posts a learning example in a study group chat. It has no name, but says “a 34-year-old with a rare genetic condition at the small unit on Skye, admitted last Tuesday”. A classmate says it is anonymous. Is it?
answers: Yes, because the name has been left out and a person’s age alone does not identify them.
Not necessarily, because rare details, place and dates together may point to one person.
Yes, provided it is only shared once and stays within a closed group of fellow students.
rationales: The risk lies in the combination of age, condition, place and date, not in any single item.
Combinations of details can identify someone even without a name. Removing the name is not the same as anonymising.
A single share or a closed group does not make information anonymous. The details are the issue, and so is the channel.
lessons.feedback: Combinations of details can identify someone even without a name. Removing the name is not the same as anonymising.

lessons.title: Explain. Listen. Repair.
lessons.description: Practise a non-judgmental loop that reveals and repairs an explanation gap.
steps: Share one manageable idea
Use plain language, then pause. Ask about preferred language, format and interpretation support. Focus on one useful next action.
Invite the person’s explanation
Say: To check that I explained it clearly, how would you describe what happens next? Frame the check around your explanation.
Repair and check again
Thank the person, identify the gap and explain it in a different way. Repeat the check until the next step is clear, using appropriate support.
lessons.outcome: Construct an explanation-check-repair loop without blame.
lessons.takeaway: Teach-back is a loop, not a yes/no question.
lessons.reflect: Which phrase will you use when the first explanation does not land?
example: A fictional patient explains a follow-up plan differently.
You were not listening.
Thank you. I need to explain that part more clearly. Let us try it another way.
Rehearse one repair phrase with a colleague.
checks: Which prompt invites teach-back?
How would you describe the next step, so I can check my explanation?
Do you understand everything?
Why did you forget?
An explanation gap appears. What next?
Rephrase the unclear part and check again.
Repeat the whole script unchanged.
Record agreement anyway.
Who is being checked in teach-back?
The clarity of the explanation and shared understanding.
The person’s intelligence.
The person’s willingness to please the team.
lessons.question: You have just explained to Mr Dean how to use his home sample kit for a bowel screening test. He looks tired, says “right, yes” and has asked nothing. The clinic is running behind. Which prompt invites teach-back?
answers: “I want to check I’ve explained that clearly. How would you describe the next step?”
“Does all of that make sense to you, or would you like me to go through it again?”
“Can you tell me the main points back, so I know that you took everything in properly?”
rationales: The prompt names your explanation as the thing being checked and asks him to say what happens next in his own words.
A yes-or-no question about understanding is easy to answer with a polite yes. Ask him to describe the step instead.
This puts the test on the listener. Asking him to prove he has listened can make people anxious and defensive.
lessons.feedback: The prompt names your explanation as the thing being checked and asks him to say what happens next in his own words.

lessons.title: Disagree without losing the purpose
lessons.description: Move from personal friction to observable concerns and a shared next step.
steps: Describe the observable issue
Separate what happened from your interpretation of motives. Use a calm statement about a specific event and its effect.
Find the shared purpose
Ask for the other perspective and name the common aim. Explore constraints without assuming that disagreement reflects poor intent.
Agree and follow through
Make a specific request, confirm an owner and arrange follow-up. Use the appropriate support or escalation route for unresolved concerns or unacceptable conduct.
lessons.outcome: Turn a personal accusation into an observable concern and a clear request.
lessons.takeaway: A useful disagreement ends with a clearer next action.
lessons.reflect: Which assumption about a colleague could you replace with a question?
example: A fictional handover lacks a named task owner.
You never take responsibility.
This task has no named owner. Can we agree who will act and when?
Rephrase one accusation as an observation and request.
checks: Which opening keeps a disagreement actionable?
The task has no named owner; can we clarify responsibility?
You never care about the team.
Everyone knows who is at fault.
A colleague offers a different account. What helps?
Explore their observations and the shared goal.
Dismiss it because your account came first.
Infer their motives.
A serious concern remains unresolved. What next?
Use the appropriate organisational escalation or support route.
Treat agreement as more important than safety.
Keep repeating a personal accusation.
lessons.question: At the 07:30 handover, two nurses disagree about who is chasing a patient’s scan result. You raise it with Dan, who said yesterday that he would. Several colleagues are listening. Which opening keeps the disagreement actionable?
answers: “You said you’d chase it yesterday and didn’t, so this keeps happening whenever it’s your turn.”
“I’m sure nobody means to leave things without an owner, so let’s not make a thing of it.”
“The scan result has no named owner on the sheet. Can we agree who is chasing it?”
rationales: It links the problem to Dan’s character, which tends to prompt defence. Describe the missing owner instead.
Smoothing it over avoids the awkwardness but leaves the scan result with no owner. Name the gap kindly and ask for an agreement.
It describes what you can see, makes no judgement about motive, and invites a specific agreement.
lessons.feedback: It describes what you can see, makes no judgement about motive, and invites a specific agreement.

lessons.title: Write so the next person can act
lessons.description: Separate facts, decisions and responsibility in a concise learning note.
steps: Record what was observed
Use relevant, accurate observations and the time or source where appropriate. Distinguish a person’s account, your observation and an interpretation.
Make the plan actionable
Include the agreed action, responsible person, timing and unresolved questions according to your local documentation requirements.
Check the receiving view
Ask whether another authorised colleague could identify what to do next. Correct errors through the approved record process; documentation does not replace urgent communication.
lessons.outcome: Identify missing ownership and uncertainty in a fictional note.
lessons.takeaway: A record should make the next action easier to understand.
lessons.reflect: What does your next colleague need from a note that you sometimes omit?
example: A fictional note reads: team aware, follow up later.
The team has been told.
I will record the agreed action, named owner, timing and any outstanding question in the approved record.
Check one fictional note for a missing owner or time.
checks: What is missing from team aware, follow up later?
An explicit action owner and timing.
More reassuring wording.
A longer paragraph.
Which sentence separates observation from interpretation?
I observed a change; I am concerned it needs review.
This must be the only possible explanation.
It is obviously fine.
Is writing an urgent concern enough?
No; use the appropriate direct escalation as well.
Yes, if the note is long.
Yes, if the record has a timestamp.
lessons.question: You pick up a patient’s notes at the start of a late shift. The last entry, written at 14:20 by a colleague who has gone home, reads: “Team aware. Follow up later.” You are not sure what, if anything, you should do. What is missing from the entry?
answers: A fuller account of what was discussed with the team, and who was present at the time.
A named person who will act on it and a time by which it should happen.
A list of the staff who were told, so the team can see exactly who is already aware of it.
rationales: More detail about the discussion could help, but without an owner and timing the next person still does not know who must act.
A record that someone else can act on has an owner and a time. “Follow up later” could mean anyone, at any time.
Naming who knows is not the same as naming who acts. Awareness without ownership leaves the task unclaimed.
lessons.feedback: A record that someone else can act on has an owner and a time. “Follow up later” could mean anyone, at any time.

lessons.title: Have a balanced risk conversation
lessons.description: Use consistent numbers, honest uncertainty and the person’s priorities.
steps: Make the comparison fair
Use the same denominator, time horizon and outcome for benefits and harms. Include the baseline and avoid relative percentages on their own.
Check what the number means
Invite the person to describe their interpretation. A visual display can support a conversation, but it does not replace accessible explanation.
Connect to what matters
Explore the person’s preferences, practical burden and need for more information. Involve the responsible clinician and arrange a way to revisit the decision.
lessons.outcome: Explain a fictional risk comparison without exaggerating benefit.
lessons.takeaway: Balanced numbers support a decision; they do not choose it for the person.
lessons.reflect: What matters to this person beyond the outcome percentage?
example: A fictional option reduces an outcome from 10 in 100 to 8 in 100.
It cuts the risk by 20%, so it is clearly best.
In this example that is 2 fewer people in 100 over the same period. Let us compare burdens and uncertainty too.
Practise a same-denominator risk explanation.
checks: A fictional outcome changes from 10/100 to 8/100. Which explanation is balanced?
2 fewer in 100 over the same period, alongside harms and uncertainty.
A 20% change with no baseline.
80 fewer people in 100.
What should accompany a visual risk chart?
An accessible explanation and a check of interpretation.
A statement that the chart chooses the best option.
A promise of individual benefit.
A person prioritises a different burden. What next?
Explore that priority with the responsible clinician.
Repeat the percentage until they agree.
Assume they misunderstood because they disagree.
lessons.question: A leaflet says a medicine “cuts the risk of an event by 20%”. In the study, the event happened in 10 per 100 people without it and 8 per 100 people with it, over the same year. A patient asks you to explain. Which explanation is balanced?
answers: A 20% reduction, which is the standard and widely understood way of describing the benefit.
8 in 100 had the event, so the other 92 in 100 were protected by taking the medicine.
2 fewer in 100 had the event that year, set alongside the possible side effects and the uncertainty.
rationales: A relative figure on its own hides the baseline. “20%” could mean 2 in 100 or 20 in 100 depending on where you start.
Many of those 92 would not have had the event anyway. Counting them all as protected overstates the benefit.
It uses the same denominator and time frame, states the baseline and puts harms alongside benefits.
lessons.feedback: It uses the same denominator and time frame, states the baseline and puts harms alongside benefits.

lessons.title: Feedback that leads somewhere
lessons.description: Describe behaviour, invite perspective and agree a small next experiment.
steps: Choose a useful moment
Use a respectful setting and clarify the learning purpose. Address urgent safety concerns immediately through the appropriate route rather than saving them for routine feedback.
Be specific and curious
Describe an observable behaviour and its effect. Ask how the other person saw the situation before offering a conclusion. Avoid labels about character.
Agree a next step
Choose a manageable behaviour to try, the support needed and a time to review. Feedback becomes useful when it changes what can happen next.
lessons.outcome: Write behaviour-focused feedback with an agreed next step.
lessons.takeaway: Useful feedback gives someone something specific they can try.
lessons.reflect: How could your next feedback include an invitation to respond?
example: In a fictional rehearsal, ownership was omitted at handover.
You are bad at handovers.
The action owner was missing. How did you see that moment, and could we practise an explicit closing request?
Give one specific observation and invite a response.
checks: Which feedback is most actionable?
The owner was unclear; let us practise naming one.
You are careless.
Try to be better.
Why invite the learner’s perspective?
It can reveal context and shape a useful next step.
It guarantees agreement.
It removes the need to discuss impact.
What completes a feedback conversation?
An agreed action, support and review point.
A label about personality.
A score without explanation.
lessons.question: You supervise a student nurse who forgot to name an owner for a task at handover. You have ten minutes at the end of the shift, and she is tired and a little anxious. Which feedback is most actionable?
answers: “At handover, nobody was named for the review. Let’s practise saying who will do it.”
“You need to be more careful with handovers, because the detail really matters in this job.”
“That was a decent effort overall, and with a bit more practice I’m sure you will get there.”
rationales: It describes an observable behaviour and offers something specific to try next.
This is a general comment about care that gives no specific behaviour to change.
Kind and encouraging, but vague. The student cannot tell what to keep doing or what to change.
lessons.feedback: It describes an observable behaviour and offers something specific to try next.

lessons.title: Turn an event into team learning
lessons.description: Compare expectations with events, identify conditions and close the learning loop.
steps: Create a respectful purpose
Clarify that the discussion aims to learn and improve. Use the appropriate formal reporting or investigation process where required. Do not include confidential case details in this app.
Compare plan and reality
Ask what was expected, what happened, what helped and what made the task difficult. Invite different roles and distinguish facts from assumptions.
Choose a follow-through
Agree one improvement question or action with a named owner and review date. Share learning through approved channels and arrange support when needed.
lessons.outcome: Structure a short debrief with one owned improvement action.
lessons.takeaway: A debrief needs both curiosity and follow-through.
lessons.reflect: Which action from a recent learning discussion still needs an owner?
example: A fictional team finishes a challenging practice session.
We finished, so there is nothing to discuss.
What helped, what was difficult, and which one change will we review next time?
Close a debrief with one named learning action.
checks: Which question opens a useful debrief?
What did we expect, and what actually happened?
Who made us look bad?
How can we prove nothing went wrong?
A debrief identifies three ideas but no owner. What is missing?
An agreed action, owner and review point.
More ideas alone.
A longer meeting title.
Does a learning debrief replace required incident reporting?
No; follow the appropriate formal process as well.
Yes, if everyone attends.
Yes, if the discussion is supportive.
lessons.question: After a stressful resuscitation simulation, the team leader opens the debrief. The team is tired and a little tense, and two members are checking the time. Which question opens a useful debrief?
answers: “What went wrong, and who needs to do something differently next time?”
“What did we expect to happen, and what actually happened as the scenario unfolded?”
“Did everyone feel it went well enough for us to move on to the next scenario?”
rationales: It sounds constructive but assumes something went wrong and points towards individuals. Start with expectations and events.
Comparing plan and reality invites facts from every role without hunting for a culprit.
This invites a quick yes and closes down learning. A debrief needs room for what made things difficult.
lessons.feedback: Comparing plan and reality invites facts from every role without hunting for a culprit.
lessons.visualAlt: Three healthcare colleagues reflecting together on a fictional learning session.

lessons.title: Be willing to update your view
lessons.description: Hold a working explanation while staying open to information that challenges it.
steps: Name what you do not know
Distinguish a working explanation from a verified fact. State uncertainty in useful terms, including the information or review needed.
Invite a different view
Ask what does not fit and who may have another perspective. A patient, caregiver or colleague may notice something missing from the current account.
Update and communicate
Revise the explanation when evidence changes. Tell relevant people what changed and what happens next within the appropriate clinical process.
lessons.outcome: Make uncertainty explicit and invite disconfirming information.
lessons.takeaway: Changing your mind can be a sign of careful thinking.
lessons.reflect: What would make you reconsider your current explanation?
example: New information challenges a fictional team’s first view.
We have already decided.
This does not fit our earlier view. What should we reconsider and who needs to review it?
Ask what information would change an assumption.
checks: Which statement shows useful humility?
Here is my current view and the uncertainty we need to resolve.
I cannot be wrong.
No one should question a confident explanation.
A patient identifies a mismatch. What helps?
Explore it and review the working explanation.
Dismiss it because it was not in the record.
Explain why the first view must be right.
What should follow a revised explanation?
Communicate the change and next action to relevant people.
Keep the update private.
Erase the learning discussion.
lessons.question: You are the registrar presenting a patient on the ward round. Your first thought was a urine infection, but the blood results do not quite fit and the consultant is waiting for your plan. Which statement shows useful humility?
answers: “My working view is a urine infection, but the bloods don’t fit, so let’s check what else it could be.”
“I’ve seen this many times and I’m confident, so let’s only revisit it if she gets any worse.”
“It could be a urine infection, though honestly I’m not really sure about anything on this case.”
rationales: It separates a working explanation from a verified fact, names what does not fit and says what is needed next.
Experience is valuable, but treating a working view as settled invites anchoring. Leave room for what does not fit.
Broad uncertainty is hard for the team to use. Useful humility names what is unclear and what would resolve it.
lessons.feedback: It separates a working explanation from a verified fact, names what does not fit and says what is needed next.

lessons.title: Protect dignity in small moments
lessons.description: Ask permission, speak directly and make participation accessible.
steps: Address the person
Use the person’s preferred name and communication approach. Do not talk over someone to their companion or assume preferences from appearance or disability.
Make choice and privacy visible
Explain your role and the intended conversation or task. Ask permission within the applicable consent process, protect privacy and respect the person’s questions.
Adapt the interaction
Ask what support would help. Arrange approved interpretation or accessible formats and involve companions according to the person’s preferences and applicable policy.
lessons.outcome: Recognise a dignity barrier and offer a respectful alternative.
lessons.takeaway: Respect is expressed through permission, privacy and participation.
lessons.reflect: Which small routine could give a person more voice or privacy?
example: A fictional discussion addresses a companion while the patient is present.
Tell us what they need.
I would like to hear from you directly. What support would make this discussion easier?
Ask a communication preference before assuming one.
checks: A companion answers every question. What supports dignity?
Address the person directly and ask their preferred involvement.
Assume the companion should decide.
Avoid the person to save time.
What should guide communication support?
The person’s expressed needs and appropriate service support.
An assumption based on age.
The standard format regardless of need.
What makes permission meaningful in a conversation?
Explain the purpose and allow questions within the applicable process.
Treat silence as agreement in every setting.
Rely only on the room number.
lessons.question: Mrs Adeyemi, who has mild hearing loss, attends clinic with her daughter. The daughter answers every question you ask, and Mrs Adeyemi has stopped looking up. You have a full waiting room. What supports her dignity?
answers: Let the daughter answer, as she is used to speaking for her mother and it will save time.
Ask the daughter to wait outside, so that the answers come from Mrs Adeyemi on her own.
Speak directly to Mrs Adeyemi, and ask her how she would like her daughter to be involved.
rationales: Habit is not consent. Letting the daughter lead may sideline Mrs Adeyemi in her own appointment.
Excluding the daughter without asking is another assumption. Ask Mrs Adeyemi what she prefers.
Addressing her directly and asking about involvement respects her as the person receiving care.
lessons.feedback: Addressing her directly and asking about involvement respects her as the person receiving care.

lessons.title: Learn fairly from an error
lessons.description: Explore system conditions while retaining fair accountability.
steps: Begin with facts and immediate safety
Use the appropriate response, reporting and support process. Record what is known and avoid speculation about an individual’s motives.
Explore the conditions
Ask about workload, tools, interruptions, unclear responsibilities and other influences. A systems approach does not mean ignoring deliberate unsafe behaviour or professional obligations.
Create a fair learning response
Use the organisation’s established process to evaluate conduct and context fairly. Agree changes, support and follow-up rather than treating a single training reminder as the whole solution.
lessons.outcome: Distinguish system learning from blame or the absence of accountability.
lessons.takeaway: Fairness needs both context and accountability.
lessons.reflect: Which system question should come before a judgment about a person?
example: A fictional team discovers a near miss.
Find the person responsible and close the issue.
Let us establish the facts, follow the reporting process and understand the conditions fairly.
Ask how the process made the error possible.
checks: What does a systems approach require?
Understanding conditions alongside fair accountability.
Ignoring every individual action.
Blaming the newest colleague.
A near miss caused no harm. What is useful?
Report and learn through the approved process.
Assume the process is safe.
Wait for harm before reviewing.
Which response supports learning?
Investigate facts and context through an established fair process.
Publicly speculate about motives.
Replace the whole investigation with a reminder.
lessons.question: A newly qualified nurse gave a medicine a few hours late after a ward move and a missing drug chart. Her manager wants to understand what happened. What does a systems approach to the review require?
answers: Setting aside what she personally did and looking only at the system, so that no one is blamed.
Understanding the conditions around the error, together with fair accountability for individual actions.
Beginning with the newest member of the team, since inexperience is a common reason for errors.
rationales: Ignoring individual actions is not fair to anyone. A fair process looks at conduct as well as context.
A just culture balances system factors and personal accountability. Neither alone gives the full picture.
Starting with the newest person is blame by default. Begin with the facts and the conditions.
lessons.feedback: A just culture balances system factors and personal accountability. Neither alone gives the full picture.

lessons.title: Own the next action
lessons.description: Make commitments visible, surface limits and follow through.
steps: Be clear about responsibility
State what you can do within your role and what needs another person’s authority or expertise. Do not accept a task by implication when responsibility is unclear.
Make limits explicit
If a commitment cannot be met, communicate the constraint early through the appropriate route. Agree an alternative owner or contingency rather than allowing a silent gap.
Close the commitment
Confirm the agreed action and record or communicate completion through the approved process. Make outstanding items visible at transition.
lessons.outcome: Turn an implied task into a clear commitment or escalation.
lessons.takeaway: Accountability includes saying when a task needs help.
lessons.reflect: Which commitment needs an explicit owner, deadline or contingency?
example: A fictional colleague assumes someone will arrange a review.
Somebody will handle it.
Let us confirm who owns the action, by when, and what happens if they cannot complete it.
Close one handover with named responsibility.
checks: A task is beyond your authority. What is accountable?
Clarify the limit and route it to the appropriate responsible person.
Accept silently and improvise.
Ignore it without communicating.
You cannot meet an agreed timing. What helps?
Communicate early and agree a safe alternative or escalation.
Wait until someone notices.
Mark it complete to avoid concern.
At transition, an item is unfinished. What next?
Make its status and receiving owner explicit.
Assume the next team will find it.
Delete it from the discussion.
lessons.question: A senior colleague asks you, a support worker, to update a patient’s care plan after a risk assessment. Only a registered nurse can sign that off, and she has to rush to a call bell. What is the accountable response?
answers: Do it carefully using your best judgement, as it needs doing and she has asked you.
Say you will have a look at it, then leave it unless she brings it up again later.
Say it is outside your role, ask who can do it, and make sure that person is told.
rationales: Willingness is admirable, but doing it beyond your authority puts the patient and you at risk.
A vague acceptance leaves a silent gap. Say clearly what you cannot do and who can.
Accountability includes recognising the limit and routing the task to the right person.
lessons.feedback: Accountability includes recognising the limit and routing the task to the right person.

lessons.title: Care with compassion and boundaries
lessons.description: Acknowledge distress while offering realistic support within your role.
steps: Notice and acknowledge
Ask what is difficult and listen without judgment. Avoid promises that are outside your control or assumptions about what another person needs.
Offer a bounded response
Explain what you can help with and what needs a different service or professional. Clear boundaries can make support more reliable.
Include the working conditions
For persistent strain, use appropriate supervisory, occupational-health or qualified support. A short personal reset does not replace workload review or organisational responsibility.
lessons.outcome: Offer an empathetic response with a realistic next step and boundary.
lessons.takeaway: Compassion can be warm, practical and honest about limits.
lessons.reflect: Where would a clearer boundary make your support more dependable?
example: A fictional colleague is struggling with continuing workload.
A quick breathing exercise will fix it.
I can listen and help identify support. We should also raise the workload concern through the appropriate route.
Identify one realistic support action and one limit.
checks: Which response is compassionate and realistic?
I can help with this step and connect you with the right support.
I promise everything will be fine.
You just need to be stronger.
What does a short reset address?
A possible momentary pause, not persistent workload problems.
Every cause of workplace distress.
The need for organisational support.
A support need exceeds your role. What helps?
Acknowledge it and connect to appropriate qualified support.
Promise unlimited availability.
Try an unfamiliar intervention without support.
lessons.question: A distressed relative stops you in the corridor and asks you, a healthcare assistant, to promise that her mother will not die this week. You have no information about the prognosis. Which response is compassionate and realistic?
answers: “I can see how frightened you are. I can’t promise that, but I can ask the nurse to talk to you.”
“I’m sure she will be fine. She is in the best place and we are looking after her very well.”
“Lots of families feel like this at first. It really helps if you can try to stay strong for her.”
rationales: It acknowledges her fear, is honest about your limits and offers something you can really do.
Reassurance you cannot back up may feel kind now but can hurt later. Be honest about what you can say.
It plays down her feelings and puts pressure on her to cope. Acknowledge the fear instead.
lessons.feedback: It acknowledges her fear, is honest about your limits and offers something you can really do.

lessons.title: Invite the voice you have not heard
lessons.description: Make participation possible across roles, communication needs and power differences.
steps: Notice who is missing
Ask which roles and perspectives are absent from a decision. Consider who cannot attend, speak easily or access the materials.
Create more than one route
Offer accessible materials and appropriate ways to contribute before, during or after the discussion. Invite concerns without putting someone on display.
Show what changed
Acknowledge contributions, explain how they influenced the decision and assign follow-up. An invitation without a response can leave people unheard.
lessons.outcome: Adapt a team discussion to include a missing perspective.
lessons.takeaway: An invitation matters more when people can see how it was used.
lessons.reflect: Whose perspective should shape your next improvement discussion?
example: A fictional meeting repeatedly hears only its most senior members.
Silence means everyone agrees.
Which perspective have we not heard, and what other way to contribute would help?
Offer a second accessible route for input.
checks: A colleague is silent in a meeting. What can you infer?
Their view is unknown; create an appropriate way to contribute.
They agree with every decision.
They have nothing useful to add.
Which meeting change supports inclusion?
Accessible materials and more than one route to contribute.
Requiring everyone to speak without preparation.
Using only the fastest discussion format.
After gathering input, what closes the loop?
Explain the decision and how contributions shaped it.
File the comments without response.
Count comments as proof of agreement.
lessons.question: At a team meeting about changing visiting hours, a healthcare assistant who usually has plenty to say stays silent throughout. The manager is keen to finish on time and records a consensus. What can you infer?
answers: They agree with the plan, otherwise they would have said so, as they usually do.
Their view is unknown, so create another way for them to contribute.
They have no strong view on the matter, so the meeting can go ahead as planned.
rationales: Assuming agreement from silence risks missing a concern. Ask in a way that is easy to answer.
Silence tells you nothing about agreement. Offering different routes for input brings out views that would be missed.
Quiet does not mean uninterested. Give them a chance to contribute before deciding.
lessons.feedback: Silence tells you nothing about agreement. Offering different routes for input brings out views that would be missed.

cases.title: The handover that almost missed it
cases.body: During a simulated shift handover, a colleague describes a patient as “stable.” You notice newly documented deterioration and the review plan is unclear. You are concerned.
cases.question: What is your best first response?
answers: Finish handover and check again later.
Clearly raise the change, request prompt clinical review, and follow the local escalation pathway.
Update the record but assume someone else will act.
cases.feedback: A concern about deterioration needs timely action within your role. State the observed change and urgency; use the local emergency response when indicated. Documentation does not replace escalation.
cases.next: The receiving clinician acknowledges your concern. What closes the loop?
nextAnswers: Confirm who will review, when, and what to do if the patient worsens or help does not arrive.
Repeat every detail from the record.
cases.nextFeedback: Shared understanding includes responsibility, timing, and a contingency plan. The handover is not complete until the next action is clear.

cases.title: “Yes, I understand.” But do they?
cases.body: In a simulated discharge conversation, a patient agrees with every explanation but cannot describe the follow-up plan. You have limited time.
cases.question: Which approach best supports understanding?
answers: Repeat the same explanation more loudly.
Ask a yes/no question one final time.
Use plain language, explain one part at a time, and invite teach-back without blame.
cases.feedback: Teach-back checks your explanation. Rephrase in smaller chunks and support language or accessibility needs.
cases.next: The patient explains part of the plan incorrectly. What next?
nextAnswers: Thank them, clarify the unclear part in a different way, then check again.
cases.nextFeedback: A misunderstanding is information for the practitioner. Re-explain, check again, and involve the appropriate support rather than labeling the patient.

cases.title: The confident answer that needs a check
cases.body: In a fictional training exercise, an AI tool produces a polished summary with a clinical claim and a reference you do not recognize.
cases.question: Before using the claim, what should happen?
answers: Verify the actual reference and claim with authoritative sources and qualified review.
Trust it because there is a citation.
Ask the tool whether it is certain and accept “yes.”
cases.feedback: AI may generate inaccurate claims or nonexistent references. A citation is a starting point for checking, not proof.
cases.next: A colleague wants to paste an identifiable patient note into an unapproved public tool. What should you advise?
nextAnswers: Remove the name; that always guarantees anonymity.
Do not share the note; use only approved workflows that meet organizational privacy and governance requirements.
Proceed if the tool is free.
cases.nextFeedback: Names are not the only identifiers. Confidential clinical information needs an approved, governed workflow, not an improvised assumption of anonymity.

cases.title: Two lists. One important pause.
cases.body: In a simulated transfer, a medication appears on one list but not another. The reason for the difference is not documented.
cases.question: What is the safest next step?
answers: Use whichever list was printed last.
Pause and clarify the discrepancy with the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
Combine both lists.
cases.feedback: An unexplained discrepancy needs reconciliation. Do not independently infer a prescribing intention or combine lists.
cases.next: The discrepancy is clarified. What supports a safer transition?
nextAnswers: Update the appropriate record, communicate the agreed plan, and check the patient’s understanding within your role.
Keep the clarification only in memory.
cases.nextFeedback: A resolution should reach the record, the next team, and the patient through the approved workflow. Clear communication prevents the discrepancy from recurring.

quotes: Better care begins with a better question.
The smallest pause can make space for the most important thing.
Knowledge informs care. Kindness makes it human.
Clarity is a form of care.
Make the safer action easier to repeat.
A concern voiced early gives the team time to respond.
One useful insight becomes stronger when you try it.
assessmentQuestions: How confident do you feel evaluating evidence and recognizing safety risks?
How confident do you feel communicating clearly and coordinating care?
How consistently can you bring curiosity, empathy, and reflection into practice?
hygieneMoments: No additional moment in this situation

hygieneScenes.title: A first introduction.
hygieneScenes.context: You approach a patient to check their pulse. You have not cleaned your hands since your previous activity. Pause before patient contact.
hygieneScenes.caption: Before contact: make the next touch a safer one.
hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 1: before touching a patient. Perform hand hygiene before contact, using the appropriate method under your local policy.

hygieneScenes.title: The bedside still counts.
hygieneScenes.context: You have adjusted the bedside table without touching the patient. You are now leaving the patient’s immediate surroundings.
hygieneScenes.caption: The patient zone includes the immediate surroundings.
hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 5: after touching patient surroundings. Contact with the patient is not required for this indication.

hygieneScenes.title: A clean task is about to begin.
hygieneScenes.context: Within your authorized role, you are about to begin an aseptic task. You have just touched the bed rail. Pause before the clean task.
hygieneScenes.caption: Before a clean task: protect the critical site.
hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 2: before a clean or aseptic procedure. Recent hand hygiene does not cover subsequent recontamination. Gloves do not replace required hand hygiene.

hygieneScenes.title: Gloves off. What comes next?
hygieneScenes.context: A task involving body-fluid exposure risk is complete. You have safely removed your gloves. No further task has started.
hygieneScenes.caption: Glove removal does not replace hand hygiene.
