hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 3: after body-fluid exposure risk. Perform hand hygiene after the task and glove removal. Use soap and water when visibly soiled and follow organism-specific and local guidance.

hygieneScenes.title: The examination is complete.
hygieneScenes.context: You have finished examining the patient and are stepping away. Pause before moving on to the wider care environment.
hygieneScenes.caption: After patient contact: protect the next interaction.
hygieneScenes.feedback: This is Moment 4: after touching a patient. One hygiene action can meet coinciding indications; the five moments do not imply duplicate cleaning back-to-back.

hygieneScenes.title: One action can be enough.
hygieneScenes.context: You have just completed appropriate hand hygiene and go directly to the patient without touching anything else. You are about to perform the planned non-aseptic examination.
hygieneScenes.caption: No new contact. No new contamination assumed.
hygieneScenes.feedback: In this specific scenario, the hand hygiene action just completed already meets Moment 1. Do not automatically repeat it without a new indication. Reassess if you touch something or the task changes.

sbarParts.name: Situation
sbarParts.text: I am the practitioner caring for this fictional patient. They have a new clinical change and need prompt review.

sbarParts.name: Background
sbarParts.text: They were transferred to our care earlier today. The change is new compared with their documented baseline.

sbarParts.name: Assessment
sbarParts.text: My observations have changed from baseline. I am concerned about deterioration and need clinical support.

sbarParts.name: Recommendation
sbarParts.text: Please arrange an appropriate review now and confirm who will attend and the immediate plan.

chest.title: Seated chest opening
chest.description: A gentle seated demonstration of opening across the chest. Stay within a comfortable range.
steps: Sit upright on a stable, armless chair, away from the backrest. Keep both feet supported.
Bring your shoulders gently back and down; extend your arms to the sides without forcing them.
Gently bring the chest forward and up. The NHS example holds for 5–10 seconds.
Return with control. Keep breathing normally; stop rather than push into pain.
chest.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes a 5–10 second hold and 5 repetitions. This player is an illustrative preview, not a prescribed routine.

march.title: Seated hip marching
march.description: Alternate a comfortable lift of each bent knee while keeping your trunk steady.
steps: Sit upright, away from the back of a stable chair. Hold the sides of the seat.
Lift one bent knee only as far as comfortable. Avoid leaning back to make the lift larger.
Lower the foot with control and settle it on the floor.
Repeat with the opposite leg. Keep the range small if that is more comfortable.
phases: Settle upright and hold the seat
Lift and lower one bent knee
Return the foot to the floor
Lift and lower the other knee
march.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes 5 lifts per leg. One illustrated loop here includes both legs; the loop counter does not count your movement.

ankle.title: Seated ankle point & flex
ankle.description: With one leg gently extended, point the toes away and draw them back within a comfortable range.
steps: Sit upright on a stable chair and hold the sides of the seat.
Straighten one leg with the foot off the floor, only if comfortable.
Point your toes away, then gently draw them back towards you. Keep the movement at the ankle.
Return with control, then use the other leg when comfortable. This illustration shows one side.
phases: Settle upright and hold the seat
ankle.sourceNote: NHS guidance describes 2 sets of 5 stretches for each foot. The illustration shows one side only; no routine is prescribed by this app.

toolIndex: Capture an insight and a next action.
Quality improvement aim, measure, balancing check, and small test.
Align the plan, adjust together, and learn
A familiar fishbone structure, with evidence checks
Practice concern, discomfort, and a safety issue.
Brief, huddle, debrief with clear ownership and changing conditions.
Watch a fictional queue, capacity, throughput, and rework model.
glossary: An invitation to explain a plan in one’s own words, helping the practitioner check their explanation.
A message is acknowledged and the agreed action, responsibility, and timing are confirmed.
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation: a structure for communicating a concern.
A starting approach to infection prevention for every patient, matched to anticipated exposure.
A shared environment where people can raise questions and concerns without humiliation.

communication.situation: A fictional patient nods during an explanation but asks the same question again.
communication.poor: You understand now, right? The leaflet explains the rest.
communication.good: I have shared a lot. To check that I explained it clearly, how would you describe the next step in your own words?
why: A yes/no question can hide uncertainty.
The stronger version makes clarity the practitioner’s responsibility.
Use an interpreter or accessible format when needed.

safety.situation: A transfer list and a fictional patient’s account disagree about a medicine.
safety.poor: This list is newer, so I will use it and leave a note.
safety.good: These accounts differ. I will clarify the discrepancy with the responsible prescriber or pharmacist through the approved process before proceeding.
why: Recency alone does not establish correctness.
Documentation does not replace resolving a discrepancy.
The next team needs the verified plan.
safety.action: Name and clarify an uncertainty before acting.

empathy.situation: A fictional patient says an agreed follow-up plan will be difficult.
empathy.poor: You need to prioritize your health and make it work.
empathy.good: What would make this plan difficult to follow? Let us understand the barrier before we agree on the next step.
why: Advice can miss cost, transport, caring responsibilities, or understanding.
A curious question invites a useful explanation.
Adaptation belongs with the appropriate care team.
empathy.action: Ask one curious question before giving more advice.

sbar.situation: During a fictional handover, the receiving colleague does not know who will arrange a review.
sbar.poor: The patient needs checking. I mentioned it earlier, so someone should follow it up.
sbar.good: The review plan is still unclear. Can we confirm who will arrange the review, the agreed timing, and what we will do if that plan is not carried out?
why: The weak version transfers information without clear ownership.
A specific request makes the next action explicit.
Urgent deterioration needs the local escalation pathway immediately.
sbar.action: Confirm an owner, timing, and contingency at handover.

infection.situation: Shared equipment is about to move from one fictional patient area to another.
infection.poor: It looks clean, and neither patient is known to have an infection.
infection.good: I will follow the approved cleaning or reprocessing process before this equipment is used again, alongside the hand hygiene and precautions appropriate to the task.
why: Appearance does not establish that equipment is ready for reuse.
Standard precautions apply to all patient care.
Follow the equipment instructions and local process.
infection.action: Clarify who prepares shared equipment for the next use.

reasoning.situation: A colleague’s first explanation does not account for new information in a fictional case.
reasoning.poor: The first explanation still sounds likely. I will wait for more convincing evidence.
reasoning.good: This new finding does not fit our current explanation. What else should we consider, and who needs to review the mismatch now?
why: New information deserves reassessment.
Distinguish observed findings from interpretation.
Seek help through the appropriate route and within your scope.
reasoning.action: Ask what does not fit the initial explanation.

speakup.situation: A junior colleague questions an assumption during a fictional team discussion.
speakup.poor: We have already considered that. Let us keep moving.
speakup.good: Thank you for raising it. Tell us what you have noticed so we can check the concern and agree on the next step.
why: A dismissive response can discourage the next concern.
Invite observable details rather than debating status.
Urgent risks still require immediate escalation.
speakup.action: Thank the next person who raises a concern.

shared.situation: A fictional patient has two reasonable options with different practical burdens.
shared.poor: Most people choose option A. It is probably the easiest decision.
shared.good: Let us compare the benefits, harms, uncertainties, and practical demands of each option. What matters most to you in making this choice?
why: A common choice may not match the individual’s priorities.
Use balanced information and current decision support.
Check understanding and involve the responsible clinician.
shared.action: Ask what matters most before closing a decision.

ai.situation: A fictional AI summary offers a confident recommendation with an unfamiliar reference.
ai.poor: It includes a citation and the wording is clear, so it is ready to use.
ai.good: I will locate the actual source, check what it supports, and use the approved review process before relying on this claim.
why: A citation may be inaccurate or fabricated.
Asking the same tool for reassurance is not independent verification.
Keep confidential material out of unapproved tools.
ai.action: Independently verify one claim and its actual source.

wellbeing.situation: A fictional colleague reports persistent fatigue affecting concentration.
wellbeing.poor: Try a short breathing exercise and push through the rest of the week.
wellbeing.good: A brief pause may help now. Let us also discuss support and workload concerns through the appropriate supervisor or occupational-health route.
why: A short exercise does not address persistent strain on its own.
Working conditions and organizational support matter.
Seek qualified support for persistent or concerning symptoms.

equity.situation: A fictional patient agrees to a plan but the team has not checked language or access needs.
equity.poor: Their family member can translate, and the standard leaflet should be enough.
equity.good: Which language and communication format work best for you? We can arrange qualified interpretation and explore practical barriers through our service.
why: Do not infer understanding from agreement.
Qualified interpretation supports communication.
Accessibility needs should shape the agreed plan.
equity.action: Ask about language and access needs without assumptions.

improvement.situation: A fictional team notices that handovers repeatedly omit ownership of pending tasks.
improvement.poor: Remind everyone to be more careful and replace the whole form next week.
improvement.good: With the team and appropriate approval, test a small ownership prompt. Define how we will measure omissions and added burden before deciding whether to adapt it.
why: A reminder alone may leave the process unchanged.
A limited test makes learning manageable.
Check intended effects and unintended burden.
improvement.action: Define one small test and a measure before trying it.

health-literacy.situation: A fictional appointment message lists several unfamiliar abbreviations.
health-literacy.poor: The instructions are standard; please read them again.
health-literacy.good: Let us put this into everyday words and identify your next step together.
why: An explanation succeeds when the person can use it.
Prioritise what the person needs to do next. Use everyday words, a short written summary and accessible formats. Ask about language and communication preferences.
health-literacy.action: Ask a person to explain the next step after one short explanation.

risk-evidence.situation: A fictional flyer says an intervention halves an outcome.
risk-evidence.poor: A 50% reduction means 50 fewer people in every 100.
risk-evidence.good: What were the starting and ending risks, time period and population?
why: Always ask: compared with what, among whom, and over how long?
In a fictional example, an outcome falls from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100. That is 2 percentage points less, and a 50% relative reduction. These describe the same change in different ways.
risk-evidence.action: Check the absolute figures behind one relative-risk claim.

human-factors.situation: A fictional team misses a task after repeated interruptions.
human-factors.good: Let us map the interruption and test a visible task cue with a named owner.
why: A reliable process supports people when attention and memory are stretched.
Reduce unnecessary complexity. Use a visible task owner, a clear cue or an approved checklist at the point of work. A reminder to concentrate is a weak response to a recurring design problem.
human-factors.action: Map one fragile step with the people who perform it.

med-transitions.situation: Two fictional lists disagree about whether Medicine A is current.
med-transitions.poor: The newest list must be right.
med-transitions.good: The accounts conflict. I will seek verification through the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
why: A discrepancy is a question to resolve, not an instruction to guess.
Record the uncertainty and route it to the responsible clinician or pharmacist. Do not decide to start, stop or change a medicine from this learning exercise.
med-transitions.action: Clarify ownership of a reconciliation question.

deterioration.situation: A fictional record says stable but new information is concerning.
deterioration.poor: The earlier note was reassuring, so I will wait.
deterioration.good: There is a new change and I am concerned. I will activate the appropriate local response now.
why: Communicate significant concern before certainty arrives.
For urgent concern, use the local emergency or escalation pathway immediately. A communication mnemonic must not become a waiting sequence or substitute for clinical assessment.
deterioration.action: Review where to find your local escalation pathway.

data-stewardship.situation: A fictional note without a name is proposed for a public tool.
data-stewardship.poor: No name means no privacy concern.
data-stewardship.good: Other details may identify the person; we need an approved workflow before sharing.
why: Useful information still needs an authorised purpose and destination.
Names are not the only identifiers. Dates, locations, rare details and combinations can identify someone. Removing a name alone does not establish anonymity.
data-stewardship.action: Identify the approved information-governance contact for your setting.

teachback-skill.situation: A fictional patient explains a follow-up plan differently.
teachback-skill.good: Thank you. I need to explain that part more clearly. Let us try it another way.
why: Teach-back is a loop, not a yes/no question.
Say: To check that I explained it clearly, how would you describe what happens next? Frame the check around your explanation.
teachback-skill.action: Rehearse one repair phrase with a colleague.

conflict.situation: A fictional handover lacks a named task owner.
conflict.good: This task has no named owner. Can we agree who will act and when?
why: A useful disagreement ends with a clearer next action.
Ask for the other perspective and name the common aim. Explore constraints without assuming that disagreement reflects poor intent.
conflict.action: Rephrase one accusation as an observation and request.

documentation.situation: A fictional note reads: team aware, follow up later.
documentation.good: I will record the agreed action, named owner, timing and any outstanding question in the approved record.
why: A record should make the next action easier to understand.
Include the agreed action, responsible person, timing and unresolved questions according to your local documentation requirements.
documentation.action: Check one fictional note for a missing owner or time.

risk-dialogue.situation: A fictional option reduces an outcome from 10 in 100 to 8 in 100.
risk-dialogue.poor: It cuts the risk by 20%, so it is clearly best.
risk-dialogue.good: In this example that is 2 fewer people in 100 over the same period. Let us compare burdens and uncertainty too.
why: Balanced numbers support a decision; they do not choose it for the person.
Invite the person to describe their interpretation. A visual display can support a conversation, but it does not replace accessible explanation.

feedback.situation: In a fictional rehearsal, ownership was omitted at handover.
feedback.good: The action owner was missing. How did you see that moment, and could we practise an explicit closing request?
why: Useful feedback gives someone something specific they can try.
Describe an observable behaviour and its effect. Ask how the other person saw the situation before offering a conclusion. Avoid labels about character.
feedback.action: Give one specific observation and invite a response.

debrief.situation: A fictional team finishes a challenging practice session.
debrief.poor: We finished, so there is nothing to discuss.
debrief.good: What helped, what was difficult, and which one change will we review next time?
why: A debrief needs both curiosity and follow-through.
Ask what was expected, what happened, what helped and what made the task difficult. Invite different roles and distinguish facts from assumptions.
debrief.action: Close a debrief with one named learning action.

humility.situation: New information challenges a fictional team’s first view.
humility.good: This does not fit our earlier view. What should we reconsider and who needs to review it?
why: Changing your mind can be a sign of careful thinking.
Ask what does not fit and who may have another perspective. A patient, caregiver or colleague may notice something missing from the current account.
humility.action: Ask what information would change an assumption.

dignity.situation: A fictional discussion addresses a companion while the patient is present.
dignity.good: I would like to hear from you directly. What support would make this discussion easier?
why: Respect is expressed through permission, privacy and participation.
Explain your role and the intended conversation or task. Ask permission within the applicable consent process, protect privacy and respect the person’s questions.
dignity.action: Ask a communication preference before assuming one.

just-culture.situation: A fictional team discovers a near miss.
just-culture.poor: Find the person responsible and close the issue.
just-culture.good: Let us establish the facts, follow the reporting process and understand the conditions fairly.
why: Fairness needs both context and accountability.
Ask about workload, tools, interruptions, unclear responsibilities and other influences. A systems approach does not mean ignoring deliberate unsafe behaviour or professional obligations.
just-culture.action: Ask how the process made the error possible.

accountability.situation: A fictional colleague assumes someone will arrange a review.
accountability.good: Let us confirm who owns the action, by when, and what happens if they cannot complete it.
why: Accountability includes saying when a task needs help.
If a commitment cannot be met, communicate the constraint early through the appropriate route. Agree an alternative owner or contingency rather than allowing a silent gap.
accountability.action: Close one handover with named responsibility.

compassion-boundaries.situation: A fictional colleague is struggling with continuing workload.
compassion-boundaries.poor: A quick breathing exercise will fix it.
compassion-boundaries.good: I can listen and help identify support. We should also raise the workload concern through the appropriate route.
why: Compassion can be warm, practical and honest about limits.
Explain what you can help with and what needs a different service or professional. Clear boundaries can make support more reliable.
compassion-boundaries.action: Identify one realistic support action and one limit.

inclusive-leadership.situation: A fictional meeting repeatedly hears only its most senior members.
inclusive-leadership.good: Which perspective have we not heard, and what other way to contribute would help?
why: An invitation matters more when people can see how it was used.
Offer accessible materials and appropriate ways to contribute before, during or after the discussion. Invite concerns without putting someone on display.
inclusive-leadership.action: Offer a second accessible route for input.

communication: Priya, a ward nurse, has just explained a new discharge plan to Mr Okafor. His taxi is due in ten minutes and he has nodded throughout without asking anything. What most directly checks how clearly she explained the next step?
Ask, “So I know I’ve explained it well, how will you describe the plan to your daughter tonight?”
Summarise the three main points again, slowly, and ask whether he has any questions before the taxi arrives.
Give him the printed discharge summary, point out the key section and ask him to ring the ward if anything is unclear.
Asking him to put the plan in his own words puts the check on your explanation, not on him. Any gap shows while he is still on the ward and you can fix it.
A slower repeat feels thorough, but “any questions?” invites a polite no. Nodding is not evidence of understanding, so try a teach-back prompt instead.
Written information helps later, but it cannot show what he has understood now. Use the leaflet to support a teach-back check rather than to replace one.
safety: A man arrives on the ward from a care home. The transfer sheet lists a blood-thinning tablet that his daughter says was stopped last week, and the GP summary does not mention it. The drug round starts in ten minutes. What best addresses the uncertainty?
Go with the transfer sheet, since it is the most formal document, and note the daughter’s comment in his file.
Ask him which tablets he took this morning and follow his account, as it is the most recent information.
Hold that item and ask the pharmacist or prescriber to reconcile the three sources before it is given.
A formal document can still be out of date. Recording the daughter’s comment without acting on it leaves the discrepancy unresolved.
His account matters, but memory and confusion on transfer can both mislead. It is one source to compare, not the tie-breaker.
Reconciliation resolves a conflict between records and the patient’s account; it does not pick a winner by guesswork. Pausing the one uncertain item protects him while the answer is found.
empathy: Mrs Hughes, 78, was given a new daily exercise plan after her fall. At review she sighs and says, “It’s all a bit much, really.” You have ten minutes. What is the most useful response before you offer any solution?
“Let’s cut it down to the easiest exercises so it feels more manageable for you.”
“It sounds like a lot to manage. Which part is hardest at the moment?”
“I know it’s hard, but sticking with it is what will get you back on your feet.”
Trimming the plan may be right in the end, but offering it first guesses at the problem. It might be the pain, the time or the stairs.
Naming the feeling and asking which part is hard shows you are curious rather than assuming. Her answer then tells you where to adapt the plan.
Explaining why the plan matters can sound like a reprimand. Understand what is getting in her way before making the case for the plan.
sbar: At 02:00 you give an SBAR about a patient whose breathing has worsened. The on-call doctor says, “OK, noted, thanks,” and starts to hang up without saying whether she is coming. What best establishes a shared plan?
“Thanks. I will record in the notes that you have been informed about his breathing, with the time of this call.”
“Just to be sure it was clear: his breathing is faster than an hour ago and he is looking more tired.”
“Before you go, who will see him and by when, and who should I call if he worsens before then?”
Documenting the call is useful but does not tell you who will act. A record that someone was informed is not a plan.
Repeating the findings checks that the message was heard, not that anyone will respond. The recommendation and ownership are what is still missing.
Ownership, timing and a contingency turn an acknowledged message into a shared plan. Asking before she hangs up is the last chance to close the loop.
infection: Between two patients on a bay, the shared blood-pressure cuff looks spotless. The first patient had no known infection and the next is waiting. What determines whether it is ready to reuse?
The cleaning or reprocessing step your local policy sets for that equipment between patients.
Whether the first patient was on additional precautions, since only then does the cuff need cleaning.
Whether anything visible is on it, because a clean-looking cuff has not touched anything harmful.
Standard precautions apply to everyone, so reuse follows the approved process for that item, not how it looks or who used it.
Waiting for an infection label misses the point of standard precautions. Equipment is prepared for reuse in the same way for every patient.
Contamination is often invisible. A visual check cannot replace the approved cleaning process.
reasoning: A man in the emergency department was labelled “anxiety, chest tightness” at triage. An hour later his observations have changed and he says the pain now spreads to his arm. What best supports a safe reassessment?
Take another full set of observations, and speak to the doctor only if they continue to worsen.
Tell the doctor what no longer fits the anxiety explanation and ask the team to consider what else it could be.
Ask the triage nurse whether she still thinks anxiety is the most likely explanation before going any further.
More observations are not wrong, but waiting to see a worse trend delays a concern you already have. Share the new information now.
Naming the mismatch out loud and opening up alternatives counters anchoring on the first label. It keeps the decision with the responsible team.
Asking the person who made the first judgement tends to bring back the same answer. Take the mismatch to the responsible clinician instead.
speakup: During a busy handover on a surgical ward, a newly qualified nurse interrupts to say, “I’m worried Mr Lee’s wound dressing is wetter than the chart suggests.” The consultant round starts in five minutes. What best supports speaking up?
Thank her, ask what she has seen, and have someone check the patient now before the handover carries on.
Ask her to jot the concern down so it can be discussed properly once the handover is over.
Explain the reasoning behind the current plan, then ask whether that changes her view.
Receiving a concern well is half of speaking up. Thanking her and checking straight away shows concerns are welcome and keeps the patient first.
Deferring may feel orderly, but it tells her that a safety concern can wait for a convenient moment. Quick checks cost minutes; missed ones cost far more.
Justifying the plan first can sound like “you are wrong”. Listen to what she observed before you defend anything.
shared: Mr Banks, 71, has two reasonable options for his painful knee: twelve weeks of physiotherapy or a referral for surgical opinion. He lives alone and is his wife’s main carer. What should shape the next conversation?
Which option most patients of his age and circumstances have chosen, as that is the best guide to what works.
Which option is simpler for the team to arrange and explain, so the plan runs smoothly.
How each option’s benefits, risks and uncertainty fit with his caring role and what matters to him.
What others chose says little about what he values. Popularity is not the same as fit.
Convenience for the service can quietly steer the choice. The options should be compared on his terms, with the real trade-offs.
Shared decisions bring the evidence and the person’s priorities into one conversation. His caring role may change which trade-off matters most.
ai: A colleague pastes an AI-generated summary into the team chat before your medicines safety meeting. It says a recent trial shows a benefit and cites “Hartley et al., 2023”, which nobody recognises. What is the strongest verification step?
Ask the tool for the full reference and the relevant quote, and accept it if it can supply both.
Find the original paper through a library or database and check it says what the summary claims.
Check that the journal looks credible and the year fits, then share it with a note that it needs review.
The same tool can generate a convincing reference and quote. Asking it to vouch for itself is not independent checking.
Only the source itself can show whether the claim is supported. AI tools can produce convincing citations that do not exist or say something else.
A plausible journal and date are easy to fake and say nothing about the claim. Circulating it first lets an unchecked claim spread.
wellbeing: Aisha, a healthcare assistant, tells you she has not slept properly for weeks and keeps losing track mid-task. The shift has started and the ward is short-staffed. What addresses both the immediate and the continuing concern?
Suggest a quiet break and say you will check in with how she feels at the end of the shift.
Share the trust wellbeing leaflet and ask her to pick one idea from it to try this week.
Offer help now, like a short break, and encourage her to raise the workload with her manager.
A break helps for now, but with nothing to follow up the longer-term picture is left alone. Pair the break with the conversation about workload.
Resources can help, but handing them over leaves the load on her. Individual habits do not replace safe staffing and rest.
Fatigue is a signal, not a flaw. Immediate support helps today, and the manager conversation addresses the conditions behind it.
equity: Mr Nowak agrees to a new monitoring plan through his adult son, who speaks for him at the surgery. Nobody has asked about language, reading or how he gets to appointments. What is the best next step?
Ask Mr Nowak how he likes to receive information and whether an interpreter would help.
Give him the standard leaflet and ask his son to go through it with him when they get home.
Check he is happy to continue in English, then book the follow-up appointment if he says yes.
Asking him directly puts him at the centre and uncovers communication and access needs that his agreement may be hiding.
This assumes the leaflet and his son will suffice. A family member can help, but is not a substitute for qualified support or for asking him.
Asking is a good start, but a polite yes may reflect reluctance to be a bother. Explore what support would help, including practical access.
improvement: Task owners are often not named at handover on your ward. The manager suggests adding a mandatory “owner” column to the handover sheet across the whole hospital next month. Which next step supports learning from a small test?
Roll the new column out across the service and ask staff for feedback after a month.
Try a limited change on one shift for two weeks, with a measure and a check for added time.
Repeat the handover refresher session and count how many staff attend.
A wide launch gives you opinions, but little evidence of whether it helped or caused problems. Test on a small scale first.
A small, time-limited test with a measure and a balancing check lets you learn what works before committing the whole service.
Counting attendance measures activity, not whether owners are being named. Choose a measure that shows the effect you want.
health-literacy: During a discharge talk at 16:30, a woman who has followed everything so far goes quiet when you say “PRN”, “U&Es” and “OPD follow-up”. She has her coat on and her lift is waiting outside. What helps most?
Swap the abbreviations for everyday words, focus on one next action, and ask her to say it back.
Slow down and say the abbreviations more clearly, so she can pick up the terms as you go along.
Carry on at the same pace, since she was following well and has not asked you to stop or explain.
Plain words, one clear action and a teach-back check make the explanation usable. Her sudden quiet may be the only sign she has lost the thread.
Slower jargon is still jargon. Replacing the terms with everyday words helps far more than repeating them.
Silence after unfamiliar terms is often confusion in disguise. Agreement or quiet is not evidence of understanding, and many people will not interrupt.
risk-evidence: A leaflet for a new screening test says it “halves the chance of a serious complication”. The study behind it shows the risk falling from 4 in 100 to 2 in 100 over five years. A patient asks what the actual reduction is. What do you tell her?
50 percentage points, because the risk has gone from 4 down to 2, which is half of what it was.
2% of the original 4%, which is a very small proportion of the risk and only a minor change.
2 percentage points, which means 2 fewer people in every 100 over the five years.
Fifty per cent is the relative reduction, not the absolute one. Mixing them up makes the benefit look far larger than it is.
Two per cent of four is about 0.08 per cent, which is not what happened. The risk fell from 4% to 2%, a drop of 2 percentage points.
The absolute reduction is the difference between the two risks: 4 minus 2. “Halves” describes the same change in relative terms.
human-factors: On a medical ward, the end-of-shift check that bed alarms are switched on keeps being missed. Three reminder emails and a team talk have not changed it, and the night shift is starting to feel blamed. What is a useful next step?
Send a firmer reminder and ask each nurse to confirm in writing that they have read it.
Watch the task as it happens, ask staff where it gets difficult, and test a cue at that step.
Look at who was on shift when it was missed and arrange extra training for those nurses.
A stronger reminder is still a reminder. A repeated omission points to a design problem, not a concentration problem.
When reminders fail, look at the work itself. Watching it and asking those who do it reveals a fragile step a support can fix.
Singling out individuals assumes the cause is personal. If several people miss the same step, the process is the likelier culprit.
med-transitions: A resident comes back to the care home after a hospital stay. A medicine for his blood pressure is on the discharge list but is not on the care home’s own record, and the senior carer asks you what that means. What can you conclude?
The hospital probably stopped it, so the care home record is right and the discharge list can be set aside.
The care home missed it, so it should be added now, since the hospital list is the more recent document.
There is a discrepancy that needs verifying with the pharmacist or prescriber before anything changes.
This guesses at the reason. A medicine missing from one record may have been left off by mistake.
Newer does not always mean correct, and adding a medicine by inference is a prescribing decision. Ask the responsible clinician.
A mismatch is a question to resolve, not an instruction. Verification comes before any start, stop or change to a medicine.
deterioration: During a routine 20:00 handover on an older-people ward, you notice Mrs Pike’s breathing is faster and she seems newly confused. The coordinator is halfway through the SBAR for bed 12 and the oncoming team is waiting. What takes priority?
Interrupt and use the immediate local escalation pathway for Mrs Pike, then return to the handover.
Let the coordinator finish a clear SBAR for bed 12, so the handover is complete before you speak up.
Write the change on the handover sheet and make sure it is raised at the next routine review.
An urgent concern does not wait for a tidy script. Escalating first keeps the patient’s safety ahead of the handover process.
A complete handover matters, but a few minutes of delay can matter more to Mrs Pike. Communicate significant concern before certainty arrives.
A note is not a call for help. Writing it down and waiting leaves a change in condition without anyone acting on it.
data-stewardship: A student nurse posts a learning example in a study group chat. It has no name, but says “a 34-year-old with a rare genetic condition at the small unit on Skye, admitted last Tuesday”. A classmate says it is anonymous. Is it?
Yes, because the name has been left out and a person’s age alone does not identify them.
Not necessarily, because rare details, place and dates together may point to one person.
Yes, provided it is only shared once and stays within a closed group of fellow students.
The risk lies in the combination of age, condition, place and date, not in any single item.
Combinations of details can identify someone even without a name. Removing the name is not the same as anonymising.
A single share or a closed group does not make information anonymous. The details are the issue, and so is the channel.
teachback-skill: You have just explained to Mr Dean how to use his home sample kit for a bowel screening test. He looks tired, says “right, yes” and has asked nothing. The clinic is running behind. Which prompt invites teach-back?
“I want to check I’ve explained that clearly. How would you describe the next step?”
“Does all of that make sense to you, or would you like me to go through it again?”
“Can you tell me the main points back, so I know that you took everything in properly?”
The prompt names your explanation as the thing being checked and asks him to say what happens next in his own words.
A yes-or-no question about understanding is easy to answer with a polite yes. Ask him to describe the step instead.
This puts the test on the listener. Asking him to prove he has listened can make people anxious and defensive.
conflict: At the 07:30 handover, two nurses disagree about who is chasing a patient’s scan result. You raise it with Dan, who said yesterday that he would. Several colleagues are listening. Which opening keeps the disagreement actionable?
“You said you’d chase it yesterday and didn’t, so this keeps happening whenever it’s your turn.”
“I’m sure nobody means to leave things without an owner, so let’s not make a thing of it.”
“The scan result has no named owner on the sheet. Can we agree who is chasing it?”
It links the problem to Dan’s character, which tends to prompt defence. Describe the missing owner instead.
Smoothing it over avoids the awkwardness but leaves the scan result with no owner. Name the gap kindly and ask for an agreement.
It describes what you can see, makes no judgement about motive, and invites a specific agreement.
documentation: You pick up a patient’s notes at the start of a late shift. The last entry, written at 14:20 by a colleague who has gone home, reads: “Team aware. Follow up later.” You are not sure what, if anything, you should do. What is missing from the entry?
A fuller account of what was discussed with the team, and who was present at the time.
A named person who will act on it and a time by which it should happen.
A list of the staff who were told, so the team can see exactly who is already aware of it.
More detail about the discussion could help, but without an owner and timing the next person still does not know who must act.
A record that someone else can act on has an owner and a time. “Follow up later” could mean anyone, at any time.
Naming who knows is not the same as naming who acts. Awareness without ownership leaves the task unclaimed.
risk-dialogue: A leaflet says a medicine “cuts the risk of an event by 20%”. In the study, the event happened in 10 per 100 people without it and 8 per 100 people with it, over the same year. A patient asks you to explain. Which explanation is balanced?
A 20% reduction, which is the standard and widely understood way of describing the benefit.
8 in 100 had the event, so the other 92 in 100 were protected by taking the medicine.
2 fewer in 100 had the event that year, set alongside the possible side effects and the uncertainty.
A relative figure on its own hides the baseline. “20%” could mean 2 in 100 or 20 in 100 depending on where you start.
Many of those 92 would not have had the event anyway. Counting them all as protected overstates the benefit.
It uses the same denominator and time frame, states the baseline and puts harms alongside benefits.
feedback: You supervise a student nurse who forgot to name an owner for a task at handover. You have ten minutes at the end of the shift, and she is tired and a little anxious. Which feedback is most actionable?
“At handover, nobody was named for the review. Let’s practise saying who will do it.”
“You need to be more careful with handovers, because the detail really matters in this job.”
“That was a decent effort overall, and with a bit more practice I’m sure you will get there.”
It describes an observable behaviour and offers something specific to try next.
This is a general comment about care that gives no specific behaviour to change.
Kind and encouraging, but vague. The student cannot tell what to keep doing or what to change.
debrief: After a stressful resuscitation simulation, the team leader opens the debrief. The team is tired and a little tense, and two members are checking the time. Which question opens a useful debrief?
“What went wrong, and who needs to do something differently next time?”
“What did we expect to happen, and what actually happened as the scenario unfolded?”
“Did everyone feel it went well enough for us to move on to the next scenario?”
It sounds constructive but assumes something went wrong and points towards individuals. Start with expectations and events.
Comparing plan and reality invites facts from every role without hunting for a culprit.
This invites a quick yes and closes down learning. A debrief needs room for what made things difficult.
humility: You are the registrar presenting a patient on the ward round. Your first thought was a urine infection, but the blood results do not quite fit and the consultant is waiting for your plan. Which statement shows useful humility?
“My working view is a urine infection, but the bloods don’t fit, so let’s check what else it could be.”
“I’ve seen this many times and I’m confident, so let’s only revisit it if she gets any worse.”
“It could be a urine infection, though honestly I’m not really sure about anything on this case.”
It separates a working explanation from a verified fact, names what does not fit and says what is needed next.
Experience is valuable, but treating a working view as settled invites anchoring. Leave room for what does not fit.
Broad uncertainty is hard for the team to use. Useful humility names what is unclear and what would resolve it.
dignity: Mrs Adeyemi, who has mild hearing loss, attends clinic with her daughter. The daughter answers every question you ask, and Mrs Adeyemi has stopped looking up. You have a full waiting room. What supports her dignity?
Let the daughter answer, as she is used to speaking for her mother and it will save time.
Ask the daughter to wait outside, so that the answers come from Mrs Adeyemi on her own.
Speak directly to Mrs Adeyemi, and ask her how she would like her daughter to be involved.
Habit is not consent. Letting the daughter lead may sideline Mrs Adeyemi in her own appointment.
Excluding the daughter without asking is another assumption. Ask Mrs Adeyemi what she prefers.
Addressing her directly and asking about involvement respects her as the person receiving care.
just-culture: A newly qualified nurse gave a medicine a few hours late after a ward move and a missing drug chart. Her manager wants to understand what happened. What does a systems approach to the review require?
Setting aside what she personally did and looking only at the system, so that no one is blamed.
Understanding the conditions around the error, together with fair accountability for individual actions.
Beginning with the newest member of the team, since inexperience is a common reason for errors.
Ignoring individual actions is not fair to anyone. A fair process looks at conduct as well as context.
A just culture balances system factors and personal accountability. Neither alone gives the full picture.
Starting with the newest person is blame by default. Begin with the facts and the conditions.
accountability: A senior colleague asks you, a support worker, to update a patient’s care plan after a risk assessment. Only a registered nurse can sign that off, and she has to rush to a call bell. What is the accountable response?
Do it carefully using your best judgement, as it needs doing and she has asked you.
Say you will have a look at it, then leave it unless she brings it up again later.
Say it is outside your role, ask who can do it, and make sure that person is told.
Willingness is admirable, but doing it beyond your authority puts the patient and you at risk.
A vague acceptance leaves a silent gap. Say clearly what you cannot do and who can.
Accountability includes recognising the limit and routing the task to the right person.
compassion-boundaries: A distressed relative stops you in the corridor and asks you, a healthcare assistant, to promise that her mother will not die this week. You have no information about the prognosis. Which response is compassionate and realistic?
“I can see how frightened you are. I can’t promise that, but I can ask the nurse to talk to you.”
“I’m sure she will be fine. She is in the best place and we are looking after her very well.”
“Lots of families feel like this at first. It really helps if you can try to stay strong for her.”
It acknowledges her fear, is honest about your limits and offers something you can really do.
Reassurance you cannot back up may feel kind now but can hurt later. Be honest about what you can say.
It plays down her feelings and puts pressure on her to cope. Acknowledge the fear instead.
inclusive-leadership: At a team meeting about changing visiting hours, a healthcare assistant who usually has plenty to say stays silent throughout. The manager is keen to finish on time and records a consensus. What can you infer?
They agree with the plan, otherwise they would have said so, as they usually do.
Their view is unknown, so create another way for them to contribute.
They have no strong view on the matter, so the meeting can go ahead as planned.
Assuming agreement from silence risks missing a concern. Ask in a way that is easy to answer.
Silence tells you nothing about agreement. Offering different routes for input brings out views that would be missed.
Quiet does not mean uninterested. Give them a chance to contribute before deciding.

choices: Pass on the concern and ask the next colleague to arrange the review.
State the new concern, request timely review, and use local escalation.
Complete the handover record first so the review request is documented.
rationales: A concern needs explicit urgency and ownership; passing it on can leave both unclear.
Raise the observed change promptly and establish action through the appropriate route.
Documentation supports communication but must not delay urgent escalation.
handover.success: The receiving clinician acknowledges the concern but has not named who will attend.
handover.recovery: The receiving colleague says, “I thought someone else had requested the review.” The concern is still unresolved.
handover.successQ: What needs to happen before you treat this as a shared plan?
handover.recoveryQ: How do you recover the communication gap now?
handover.good: Confirm the action owner, timing, and contingency through the local route.
alternatives: Send the details in writing and assume acknowledgment is sufficient.
Wait until the next routine check before asking for an update.
handover.debrief: A handover is complete only when the relevant next action and responsibility are understood. Escalate urgent concerns immediately through local procedures.

choices: Repeat the explanation slowly, then ask whether it is clear.
Give a written summary and arrange a later opportunity for questions.
Explain one part simply, then invite the patient to describe the next step.
rationales: Slowing down can help, but a yes/no check still may not reveal understanding.
Written support is useful, but the current misunderstanding needs clarification.
A focused teach-back prompt makes the patient’s understanding visible without blame.
teachback.success: The patient describes one part correctly but confuses the follow-up arrangement.
teachback.recovery: The patient agrees again, then describes a follow-up arrangement that differs from the explanation.
teachback.successQ: How should you respond to the part that is still unclear?
teachback.recoveryQ: What would help you clarify the misunderstanding now?
teachback.good: Thank them, re-explain the unclear part differently, and invite teach-back again.
alternatives: Repeat the same wording and ask whether they understand it now.
Mark the discussion complete and rely on the written summary.
teachback.debrief: Teach-back checks the explanation. Clarify the specific gap and arrange language or accessibility support where needed.

choices: Locate the actual reference and check what it supports before using the claim.
Ask the AI tool for a fuller explanation and a confidence rating.
Compare two fresh answers from the same tool for consistency.
rationales: Independent checking tests both whether the source exists and what it actually says.
More detail or confidence from the same tool is not independent verification.
Repeated generated answers can repeat the same unsupported claim.
ai-case.success: You locate the reference, but it does not support the recommendation in the summary.
ai-case.recovery: The tool gives another confident explanation, but the underlying reference remains unverified.
ai-case.successQ: What is the most useful way to handle the unsupported claim?
ai-case.recoveryQ: How do you move from reassurance to verification?
ai-case.good: Set the claim aside and verify it through authoritative sources and approved review.
alternatives: Keep the claim but label it as AI-generated so the reader can decide.
Use the claim only in a shorter summary to reduce its prominence.
ai-case.debrief: A fluent explanation and a citation are starting points for checking. Keep qualified oversight and protect confidential information.

choices: Use the most recent list while documenting the discrepancy.
Clarify the discrepancy with the responsible clinician or pharmacist.
Use the patient’s account while waiting for the transfer team to reply.
rationales: A timestamp does not establish prescribing intention. Documenting alone does not resolve the conflict.
Reconciliation through the responsible team addresses the uncertainty.
The patient’s account is important evidence, but does not alone resolve a prescribing discrepancy.
med-case.success: The responsible team clarifies the intended plan through the approved process.
med-case.recovery: A colleague points out that the two records still show different plans. The intended plan has not been verified.
med-case.successQ: What will support a clearer transition now?
med-case.recoveryQ: What should you do with the unresolved difference?
med-case.good: Verify the plan through the responsible team, update the approved record, and communicate it.
alternatives: Keep a personal note so you can explain the difference if asked.
Leave both lists visible so the next team can choose between them.
med-case.debrief: An unexplained medication discrepancy needs reconciliation. The verified plan should reach the appropriate record, next team, and patient within your role.

sbar.title: Build a clearer handover
fields: Situation — the current concern and urgency
Background — the context that changes the next decision
Assessment — observations, concern, and uncertainty within your role
Recommendation — requested action, owner, and timing
Close the loop — acknowledgment and contingency
good: This is a fictional communication exercise. The agreed review has not yet been assigned.
The request was discussed at handover, but the receiving team has no named owner.
The unresolved issue is responsibility and timing, rather than whether the message was sent.
Please confirm who will arrange the review and the agreed timing.
We will confirm the plan back and use the approved escalation route if it is not carried out.
sbar.note: Use invented details only. Do not delay urgent escalation to draft a message. This is not a clinical record.

teach.title: Practise a teach-back conversation
fields: One point to explain in plain language
My non-judgmental teach-back invitation
A fictional response showing a gap
How I will clarify and check again
good: The next step is to contact the service using the agreed route to confirm your follow-up arrangement.
To check that I explained it clearly, how will you describe your next step in your own words?
I will wait for someone to call me, even if I do not hear back.
Thank you. I did not explain that clearly. Let us revisit how you will make contact, then check the plan together.
poor: Follow the advice in the leaflet.
teach.note: Practice with fictional details. Adapt the conversation, interpretation, and accessible formats to the person and your service.

qi.title: Plan one small improvement test
fields: The process issue — describe the system, not a person
Small test and required local approval
What I will measure and how
What unintended effect or burden I will check
Who will review the result and decide what comes next
good: Fictional handovers sometimes omit the owner of a pending task.
With the relevant team’s approval, test one ownership prompt in a limited handover exercise.
Count missing task owners before and during the fictional test, using the same definition.
Ask whether the prompt adds avoidable time or confusion.
The agreed team lead and participants will compare results and decide whether to adapt, repeat, or stop.
poor: Count staff who received an email.
qi.note: This is an editorial planning aid. Obtain appropriate local approval before changing practice. No invented benchmark or promised outcome.

cus.title: CUS speaking-up planner
fields: Concern — the observed fact and why it matters
Uncomfortable — the unresolved risk or uncertainty
Safety issue — the specific safety concern
Requested response and appropriate escalation route
good: I am concerned that the handover does not name an owner for the agreed review.
I am uncomfortable proceeding while responsibility remains unclear.
This is a safety issue because the review may be missed without an agreed owner.
Please clarify the owner and timing now. If unresolved, I will use the appropriate local escalation route.
cus.note: Fictional communication practice informed by AHRQ CUS. Urgent risks require immediate local escalation; do not wait to complete a script.

desc.title: DESC conversation planner
fields: Describe the specific observable situation
Express your concern using an I statement
Suggest an alternative and seek agreement
Consequences — explain the impact on shared goals
good: In our fictional team meeting, my question was interrupted twice before I could explain the concern.
I am concerned that we may miss relevant information when people cannot finish.
Could we agree to let each person finish, then ask clarifying questions?
This would help us understand concerns and make a clearer shared plan. Can we agree to try it?
poor: If it happens again, you will regret it.
desc.note: A fictional planning aid informed by AHRQ DESC. Use appropriate organizational support for bullying, harassment, or unsafe situations.

huddle.title: Brief, huddle & debrief board
huddle.sub: Align the plan, adjust together, and learn
fields: Shared purpose — what are we trying to achieve?
Roles — who owns each next action?
Constraints — what has changed or needs support?
Contingency — when and how will we regroup?
Debrief — what helped, what got in the way, and what will change?
good: Prepare a fictional staff-learning session with clear ownership of the remaining tasks.
Alex checks the room; Sam checks materials; Lee confirms the participant list.
The room has changed and the learning materials are still in the old location.
Regroup before the session. If materials are unavailable, use the agreed backup activity.
A brief shared check found the location gap. Next time confirm the room before moving the materials.
huddle.note: Original fictional team-learning template informed by TeamSTEPPS leadership principles. This is not a clinical staffing or acuity allocation tool.

Sender and receiver have different assumptions about who confirms ownership.

The shared template opens an older version by default.

cusScenes.title: Name the concern
cusScenes.event: In a fictional handover, a planned review has no named owner. The receiving colleague says, “It will probably be sorted.”
options: Ask whether the colleague thinks there is anything to worry about.
State the missing ownership and why you are concerned.
Assume the request was understood and add a note for later.
why: An open question can help, but the observed concern still needs to be made explicit.
The message names an observable gap and connects it to the concern.
A note does not resolve responsibility for the planned action.

cusScenes.title: Make the uncertainty explicit
cusScenes.event: Your concern has not been resolved. The colleague acknowledges the message but still does not know who owns the review.
options: Repeat that a review was mentioned during the earlier handover.
Explain that you will ask about the review at the next routine meeting.
Say you are uncomfortable proceeding while responsibility is unclear.
why: Repeating the history may leave the unresolved responsibility unchanged.
A meeting later is not a substitute for resolving a current concern through the proper route.
This makes the unresolved uncertainty explicit and invites a response.

cusScenes.title: Connect the concern to safety
cusScenes.event: Responsibility is still unclear. The fictional team needs an explicit response through its approved process.
options: State the safety concern, request a clear response, and use local escalation if unresolved.
Use more forceful wording about the colleague’s attitude so the issue gets attention.
Stop communicating because the concern has already been raised twice.
why: Link the concern to safety and use the appropriate local route. Urgent concerns must be escalated immediately.
Personal accusations distract from the observable risk and the required action.
An unresolved concern needs the appropriate response, not an arbitrary limit on communicating.

huddleTasks.name: Room preparation
huddleTasks.backup: Confirm the new room before setting up.

huddleTasks.name: Learning materials
huddleTasks.constraint: Materials are still in the old room.
huddleTasks.backup: Move them after the room is confirmed; use the backup activity if unavailable.

huddleTasks.name: Participant information
huddleTasks.constraint: The invitation still names the old room.
huddleTasks.backup: Send the confirmed location through the agreed communication route.

good: In this fictional training session, participants received two different room locations.
The booking changed after the first invitation was sent.
The conflicting messages could leave participants waiting in the wrong place.
Please confirm the correct room with the organizer and issue one clear update.
Confirm who sends the update and how participants who miss it will be directed.
poor: I sent a message, so it is finished.

good: For this fictional orientation activity, sign in at the confirmed training room before joining the group.
To check that I explained the arrangement clearly, where will you go first?
I will join the group first and sign in if there is time.
Thank you. I need to clarify the order. Sign in first, then join the group. How would you describe those steps now?
Participants in a fictional learning session sometimes receive an outdated room location.
With the organizer’s approval, test a single final-location confirmation for one session.
Count conflicting location messages using a consistent definition before and during the test.
Check whether the confirmation creates extra messages or delays the invitation.
The organizer and participants will review the results and decide whether to keep or adapt the change.
poor: Send many more reminders to everyone.
Count how many messages were sent.
More messages cannot cause any problems.
Assume attendance proves the change worked.

good: I am concerned that two fictional training participants are about to use materials labeled with different versions.
I am uncomfortable continuing until we verify which version is approved for this session.
This could create a safety-learning problem if inconsistent instructions are taught.
Please check the approved version with the responsible organizer before we proceed; escalate unresolved concerns through the relevant route.
poor: You brought the wrong files again.
I have mentioned it, so it is your problem.

good: During the fictional learning session, questions were answered before the participant finished speaking.
I am concerned that we may miss what the participant is actually asking.
Could we pause until the person finishes, then check our understanding?
This could make the discussion clearer and reduce repeated explanations. Can we try it together?
poor: You do not know how to listen.
Everyone agrees that you are rude.
Let someone else do the talking.
If you continue, I will embarrass you in front of the group.

good: Prepare a fictional orientation session using one confirmed room location and one materials version.
Ari confirms the booking; Jamie checks the materials version; Robin sends the location update.
The booking confirmation has changed and one shared folder still contains an older handout.
Regroup before distribution. Use only the version confirmed by the organizer and direct arrivals to the confirmed room.
Compare the actual arrival experience with the plan, then agree one improvement for the next session.
poor: Whoever has time can sort it out.
Changes happen; no need to discuss them.
People will ask if they are confused.
No complaints means no improvements are needed.

good: Participants in a fictional orientation receive conflicting location information.
Different organizers assume someone else sends the final confirmation.
The booking change process does not include a final invitation check.
A shared invitation template retains the prior location.
The booking changes shortly before the session, while organizers are handling other tasks.
Review the message sequence, booking-change process, and template history; ask organizers how responsibility was understood. These are possible contributors, not established causes.
poor: The whole booking system is useless.
The cause is obvious from one complaint.

communication.question: Priya, a ward nurse, has just explained a new discharge plan to Mr Okafor. His taxi is due in ten minutes and he has nodded throughout without asking anything. What most directly checks how clearly she explained the next step?
answers: Ask, “So I know I’ve explained it well, how will you describe the plan to your daughter tonight?”
Summarise the three main points again, slowly, and ask whether he has any questions before the taxi arrives.
Give him the printed discharge summary, point out the key section and ask him to ring the ward if anything is unclear.
rationales: Asking him to put the plan in his own words puts the check on your explanation, not on him. Any gap shows while he is still on the ward and you can fix it.
A slower repeat feels thorough, but “any questions?” invites a polite no. Nodding is not evidence of understanding, so try a teach-back prompt instead.
Written information helps later, but it cannot show what he has understood now. Use the leaflet to support a teach-back check rather than to replace one.

communication.question: Ms Rahman has just been told by the practice nurse that her blood test needs repeating. As she picks up her coat she says, “I still don’t know what happens next.” The next patient is already waiting. What is the most useful response?
answers: Go back over the whole conversation from the start in case she missed a detail, even if the clinic runs later.
Agree the next step aloud: who will book the test, by when, and what she should do if she hears nothing.
Point to the leaflet on the desk and invite her to phone reception once she has read it at home.
rationales: Repeating everything can bury the one thing she is missing. Find the unclear step first, then restate only that and check again.
This closes the loop. A clear next action, a named owner, a time frame and a safety-net tell her exactly what to expect.
A leaflet supports a conversation, but it leaves her question unanswered and hands the follow-up to her. Agree the plan before she leaves the room.

communication.question: A pharmacist has shown a man how to use a new inhaler device and wants to check he can manage it at home. Which wording keeps the check about her explanation rather than about him?
answers: “You’ve got the idea, haven’t you? Just tell me if there is anything you are unsure about.”
“Can you repeat back what I just told you, so I know you were listening properly?”
“I want to be sure I’ve explained this clearly. Could you show me how you’ll use it at home?”
rationales: A closed question that expects a yes makes it hard to admit confusion. Ask him to show or tell you instead.
This frames the check as a test of his attention, which can make people defensive or silent. Put the focus on how clearly you explained it.
Naming your own explanation as the thing being checked keeps the tone kind and invites an honest answer. Watching him demonstrate shows more than a verbal yes.

safety.question: A man arrives on the ward from a care home. The transfer sheet lists a blood-thinning tablet that his daughter says was stopped last week, and the GP summary does not mention it. The drug round starts in ten minutes. What best addresses the uncertainty?
answers: Go with the transfer sheet, since it is the most formal document, and note the daughter’s comment in his file.
Ask him which tablets he took this morning and follow his account, as it is the most recent information.
Hold that item and ask the pharmacist or prescriber to reconcile the three sources before it is given.
rationales: A formal document can still be out of date. Recording the daughter’s comment without acting on it leaves the discrepancy unresolved.
His account matters, but memory and confusion on transfer can both mislead. It is one source to compare, not the tie-breaker.
Reconciliation resolves a conflict between records and the patient’s account; it does not pick a winner by guesswork. Pausing the one uncertain item protects him while the answer is found.

safety.question: On an evening round, a nurse finds a prescription whose handwriting could be read as two different strengths. The prescriber has gone off shift and the next dose is due in an hour. What supports safer practice?
answers: Give the strength that matches what the patient had yesterday, and leave a note for the morning team to confirm.
Pause and contact the on-call prescriber or pharmacist through the approved route to clarify before giving it.
Ask a colleague which strength she thinks it says and give it if you both read it the same way.
rationales: Using yesterday’s pattern is a sensible-sounding guess, but a guess it remains. A note for the morning comes after the dose has gone.
If an order is unclear, stopping to clarify is the safety action. An hour leaves time to ask, so the pause costs little.
Two people agreeing is not the same as the prescriber confirming. Shared misreading is a classic way an error passes a check.

safety.question: Dev, a healthcare assistant, nearly took the wrong patient to theatre until a colleague spotted that the wristband did not match. No one was harmed, and Dev feels embarrassed. How should the event be handled so the team can learn?
answers: Report what happened, when, and what helped to catch it through the incident system, without assigning blame.
Mention it informally at handover and keep the formal report for when something actually goes wrong.
Write the report and name the colleague who handed over the patient, so the cause is clear.
rationales: A near-miss report shows where the system is fragile. Recording the facts and what caught the error lets the team fix the process before harm occurs.
An informal chat reaches only the people in the room and leaves no trace for the wider system. Near misses are the cheapest lessons you will get.
Naming a person tends to end the inquiry early and makes others less willing to report. Describe the steps and conditions instead.

empathy.question: Mrs Hughes, 78, was given a new daily exercise plan after her fall. At review she sighs and says, “It’s all a bit much, really.” You have ten minutes. What is the most useful response before you offer any solution?
answers: “Let’s cut it down to the easiest exercises so it feels more manageable for you.”
“It sounds like a lot to manage. Which part is hardest at the moment?”
“I know it’s hard, but sticking with it is what will get you back on your feet.”
rationales: Trimming the plan may be right in the end, but offering it first guesses at the problem. It might be the pain, the time or the stairs.
Naming the feeling and asking which part is hard shows you are curious rather than assuming. Her answer then tells you where to adapt the plan.
Explaining why the plan matters can sound like a reprimand. Understand what is getting in her way before making the case for the plan.

empathy.question: On a community mental health visit, Sam hesitates after you outline weekly group sessions and says, “Yeah, okay.” His shoulders drop and he glances at the door. What is the most useful next question?
answers: “Most people find the group helpful once they are there. Shall I book you in?”
“Is the time a problem? I can note that you would prefer to start later.”
“You went quiet just then. What, if anything, worries you about the group sessions?”
rationales: Reassuring him with what others experience closes the conversation before his concern is heard. Ask first, then reassure if it fits.
Guessing the barrier and offering a fix can miss the real issue, such as fear of being judged. Ask an open question to find out.
Noticing the hesitation and asking an open question lets Sam say what is really on his mind. A tentative yes is often not a real one.

empathy.question: A daughter tells you she is exhausted after a fortnight of hospital visits to her father. A call bell is sounding in the next bay and you have about a minute. Which response acknowledges her without overstepping your role?
answers: “That sounds exhausting. What would help most over the next few days?”
“You are doing brilliantly, and he is in safe hands, so try not to worry too much.”
“I understand how that feels. I will make sure someone from the team rings you each day.”
rationales: This validates the feeling and invites her priority, with no promises. It is also short enough to fit the minute you have.
Praise and reassurance mean well, but they can tell her that her feelings are not welcome. Acknowledge first, then ask what would help.
A promise outside your control sets her up for disappointment. Offer what you can actually do, and pass on the request through the right route.

sbar.question: At 02:00 you give an SBAR about a patient whose breathing has worsened. The on-call doctor says, “OK, noted, thanks,” and starts to hang up without saying whether she is coming. What best establishes a shared plan?
answers: “Thanks. I will record in the notes that you have been informed about his breathing, with the time of this call.”
“Just to be sure it was clear: his breathing is faster than an hour ago and he is looking more tired.”
“Before you go, who will see him and by when, and who should I call if he worsens before then?”
rationales: Documenting the call is useful but does not tell you who will act. A record that someone was informed is not a plan.
Repeating the findings checks that the message was heard, not that anyone will respond. The recommendation and ownership are what is still missing.
Ownership, timing and a contingency turn an acknowledged message into a shared plan. Asking before she hangs up is the last chance to close the loop.

sbar.question: A district nurse phones a GP about a patient with a hot, swollen leg. She has given the situation, background and her observations, and the GP asks, “So what are you asking me to do?” Which reply is the recommendation?
answers: “I think it could be an infection, but I can’t be certain without a doctor looking at it.”
“I would like you to visit today, or tell me if I should arrange hospital review.”
“It has been swollen for two days and he was started on antibiotics last week.”
rationales: This is your assessment of the problem, which is valuable, but it still leaves out what you want done and by when.
A recommendation states the action you need and when. It also gives the GP a clear choice to respond to.
That is background. It helps the GP picture the case but does not say what you are asking for.

sbar.question: You tell the night coordinator that a bed-bound patient’s family are asking for a senior review. She replies, “Yes, I’ve heard you,” and picks up another phone. Nobody has said who will go. What remains to do?
answers: Ask directly who will speak to the family, by what time, and what you should do if that does not happen.
Take her acknowledgement as handing it over, and tell the family a senior colleague has been informed.
Send the same message to two more senior colleagues so at least one of them picks it up.
rationales: Being heard is not the same as taking ownership. A named person, a time and a fallback complete the handover.
Acknowledgement alone does not assign the task, and telling the family it is in hand may promise something no one has agreed to.
Widening the audience spreads responsibility thinner, so everyone can assume someone else is acting. Pin down one owner instead.

infection.question: Between two patients on a bay, the shared blood-pressure cuff looks spotless. The first patient had no known infection and the next is waiting. What determines whether it is ready to reuse?
answers: The cleaning or reprocessing step your local policy sets for that equipment between patients.
Whether the first patient was on additional precautions, since only then does the cuff need cleaning.
Whether anything visible is on it, because a clean-looking cuff has not touched anything harmful.
rationales: Standard precautions apply to everyone, so reuse follows the approved process for that item, not how it looks or who used it.
Waiting for an infection label misses the point of standard precautions. Equipment is prepared for reuse in the same way for every patient.
Contamination is often invisible. A visual check cannot replace the approved cleaning process.

infection.question: A nurse has just changed a dressing and is still wearing gloves when a call bell rings in the next bay. She says, “I’ll keep these on, they’re protecting me.” What fits standard precautions?
answers: Keep them on for a quick task and clean hands at the end of the round instead.
Remove the gloves and clean hands at that moment, then put on a fresh pair for the next task.
Wipe the gloves with a sanitising wipe, which makes them safe to wear into the next bay.
rationales: Gloves can carry organisms from one patient to the next. Hand hygiene is needed at the moment of change, not later.
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Removing them and cleaning hands at the right moment protects the next patient and the nurse.
Gloves are not designed to be cleaned and reused between patients. The safe sequence is to remove them, clean hands and re-glove.

infection.question: A carer is giving oral care to a resident, wearing gloves and an apron. The resident suddenly vomits on the floor and the carer’s sleeve. What should guide the precautions she uses next?
answers: Carry on with the same precautions, since she has already started and is wearing protective equipment.
Do what her colleague did at the last spill, as that worked and saves time on checking the policy.
Reassess what she may now be exposed to and follow local guidance for body-fluid spills and clothing.
rationales: Protection chosen for oral care may not cover a spill. Starting a task is not a reason to stop reassessing.
Copying habits passes on workarounds as well as good practice. Check against the local guidance for this exposure.
When the task changes, the likely exposure changes with it. Matching precautions to the new risk is what standard precautions mean in practice.

reasoning.question: A man in the emergency department was labelled “anxiety, chest tightness” at triage. An hour later his observations have changed and he says the pain now spreads to his arm. What best supports a safe reassessment?
answers: Take another full set of observations, and speak to the doctor only if they continue to worsen.
Tell the doctor what no longer fits the anxiety explanation and ask the team to consider what else it could be.
Ask the triage nurse whether she still thinks anxiety is the most likely explanation before going any further.
rationales: More observations are not wrong, but waiting to see a worse trend delays a concern you already have. Share the new information now.
Naming the mismatch out loud and opening up alternatives counters anchoring on the first label. It keeps the decision with the responsible team.
Asking the person who made the first judgement tends to bring back the same answer. Take the mismatch to the responsible clinician instead.

reasoning.question: A GP trainee is sure a child’s fever is a simple viral illness. The mother mentions the child has not passed urine since morning, which does not fit. What is useful?
answers: Pause to ask what else could explain both, and explore the details that do not fit the viral picture.
Note the history as reported but keep to the viral plan, since viral fevers are very common at this time of year.
Ask more questions about typical viral symptoms to confirm the diagnosis before moving on.
rationales: A diagnostic pause asks what does not fit and what important alternative should not be missed. A single odd detail may be the most informative one.
Common things are common, but a common label should not replace the details in front of you. Record it and act on it.
Looking only for confirming information is a trap. Look for what would change the picture, not just reinforce it.

reasoning.question: A healthcare assistant has noticed a resident is more drowsy than at breakfast and goes to tell the nurse in charge. Which wording keeps what she saw apart from what she thinks it means?
answers: “She’s had a poor night, so she’s just tired, but I thought I should mention it anyway.”
“She’s obviously coming down with an infection. Can you get a doctor to look at her?”
“She’s sleepier than at breakfast and hard to rouse. I’m worried it may be more than tiredness.”
rationales: This slips an explanation in as if it were a fact and quietly plays down what she saw. Give the observation and let the nurse assess.
